Nearly 75pc of Canadian exports head to the US market, and the US economy is roughly 10 times larger. Meanwhile, the new sweeping tariff slate covers another C$28bn (£15bn) worth of Canadian exports – equivalent to 5pc of products sent south of the border.
The spat escalated further on Monday, with Donald Trump promising that a 50pc tariff on Canadian cars, trucks, and auto parts will kick in from Jan 1 2027.
This comes at a time when 3pc inflation means ordinary Canadians are experiencing many of the same cost of living pressures as other parts of the world, particularly when it comes to groceries. Food inflation in Canada is the highest in the G7.
So for all his bravado, Carney could soon be forced to adopt a more conciliatory tone.
At the same time, however, the human bulldozer that is Trump may eventually come to regret this latest incursion, in the same way that his war with Iran has proven to be a massive miscalculation – militarily, economically and politically.
Whenever Trump turns his trade bazooka on another country, his working assumption is that the other side will always cave in because there is an inherent mismatch with the world’s largest economy that means its partners stand to suffer far greater losses.
Yet Carney has called his bluff at a time when Trump has never been more vulnerable, partly because of the costly fallout from Washington’s protracted and failing war in the Middle East.
It’s a big gamble on the Canadian prime minister’s part, but he will have almost certainly spotted that Americans’ disillusionment with Trump is growing as an increasing number of ordinary voters say their financial struggles are becoming more acute.
For many Americans, a full-blown trade war risks having a very notable effect on their day-to-day cost of living, which explains the obvious angst among senior politicians across the US political spectrum.
Gretchen Whitmer, the Democratic governor of Michigan, which borders Canada and is home to the American car industry, said her state was “uniquely impacted” by “the tariff wars” with Ottawa.
Fresh levies amounted to a “tax hike on Michigan families and businesses by raising prices at the grocery store and the gas pump”, she posted on X.
Companies – especially the big car manufacturers – would be forced to take “the difficult decision of laying off workers or passing costs on to their customers”, Whitmer added.
Abigail Spanberger, the Virginia governor, also a Democrat, pointed out that Canada was the state’s biggest export destination. Fresh tariffs would “hurt Virginia families, farmers, producers, foresters and businesses” in “a matter of days”, she warned.
But it was telling that the backlash wasn’t confined to Trump’s opponents. Susan Collins, a Republican senator from Maine, which shares a border with Canada, said the tariffs would “increase costs for Maine families, as most businesses will have no choice but to pass on the tariffs to their customers through higher prices”.
Mike Pence, Trump’s first-term vice-president, waded in as well, telling CNN: “The last thing we need right now, as our economy is getting back on its feet, is a trade war with Canada.” The intervention is unlikely to have gone down well in the White House.
Nor will a man who has little time for central bankers appreciate the contribution of Neel Kashkari, the president of the Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis, who warned that inflation would become more entrenched as a result of “back and forth on the trade front”.
Some prominent Republicans remain reluctant to criticise Trump. Greg Abbott, the governor of Texas, told ABC News on Friday that “people are not talking to me about Trump” on the campaign trail. He also claimed Trump was “on a track” to “have prices lowered”.
Yet that’s not what the polls are saying as five months of conflict in Iran take their toll, driving up energy prices and further prolonging several years of above-target inflation.
Although US inflation eased for a second month in July, with consumer price rises coming in at 3.4pc from a year earlier, it has remained above the Fed’s target for more than five years, stoking fears among US central bankers that high prices could become embedded in the economy.
It explains why multiple polls reveal an electorate that is deeply pessimistic about the country’s economic prospects. A survey conducted by the non-partisan market research firm SSRS for CNN found more than 75pc of Americans rate the economy as performing poorly.
Polls by the Pew Research Center and Fox News registered similar responses, which is why it is no surprise that Trump’s approval rating is at rock bottom.
With mid-term elections around the corner, and the economy always a defining issue for this crucial point in the election cycle, Trump has chosen a spectacularly bad time to pick a fight with one of his most important trading partners.
The prevailing assumption seems to be that Canada has by far the most to lose from a trade war with the US, yet it’s not quite as one-sided as some think.
According to Paul Krugman, the Nobel Prize-winning economist, the US economy is “far more dependent on Canadian goods than most Americans realise”.
He points to softwood lumber that is used by many housebuilders for framing, electricity from Canadian hydropower and US-Canadian trade in cars and car parts, as areas of particular vulnerability.
He, along with David Blackmon, an energy consultant, also highlights the US economy’s heavy reliance on imports of Canadian oil as another serious weakness.
Blackmon points out that the US imports around four million barrels of Canadian crude every single day – the vast bulk of it heavy, sour grades from Alberta’s oil sands that refiners can’t easily replace with lighter versions from the Permian basin of Texas or the waters of the Gulf of Mexico.
Carney has something else too, which could prove even more decisive: the firm backing of his people.
In a poll conducted just days before talks collapsed, 56pc of Canadians said they wanted the government to take a hard line and make no more concessions, a position that has only hardened after Washington’s more extraordinary demands were made public.
The US was trying to restrict Canada’s ability to make deals with other trading partners, and its negotiators tried to restrict Canada’s protections for the French language, Carney told reporters. Within hours, a new survey showed 76pc supported the ending of talks.
The Toronto Star likened the US approach to “an attempted psychological annexation that could have turned Canada into an American client state, a sort of North American Belarus”. Carney has called it “a question of sovereignty”.
With ordinary Canadians seemingly well up for the fight, in contrast to their battle-weary American cousins, this may be another war Trump comes to quickly regret.
summary: Trade talks between the US and Canada have broken down, leading to escalating tariffs and a brewing economic conflict initiated by Donald Trump. While Canada is significantly smaller economically, the trade war threatens to increase the cost of living for Americans and risks backfiring on Trump amid low approval ratings and ongoing inflation. Prominent figures from both political parties, governors, and economists have warned that the tariffs will harm domestic consumers, manufacturers, and families.
key_points: Donald Trump promised a 50pc tariff on Canadian cars, trucks, and auto parts starting January 1, 2027.
Nearly 75pc of Canadian exports go to the US, but the US economy is also heavily dependent on Canadian goods, including crude oil, electricity, and lumber.

Bipartisan backlash has emerged in the US, with governors like Gretchen Whitmer and Abigail Spanberger, along with politicians like Susan Collins and Mike Pence, warning that tariffs will raise costs for American families.
Over 75pc of Americans rate the economy as performing poorly, and Trump's approval ratings are low as mid-term elections approach.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has strong public backing, with surveys showing 76pc support for ending the trade talks.

title: Trump claims US could rename Lake Ontario as Lake America amid Canada trade war – live
author: Shrai Popat; Hayden Vernon; Tom Perkins
content:
Trump claims US could rename Lake Ontario as Lake America amid Canada trade war – live
Lake Ontario lies on the border between the two countries, with New York state on one side and Toronto, the capital of Canada’s Ontario province, on the other
Trump claims US could rename Lake Ontario as Lake America amid Canada trade war
Donald Trump has claimed he is considering renaming Lake Ontario as “Lake America” as the trade war with Canada escalates.
Lake Ontario lies on the border between the two countries, with New York state on one side and Toronto, the capital of Canada’s Ontario province, on the other.
“The United States is giving serious consideration to changing the name of Lake Ontario to Lake America in that we don’t expect to doing much business with Ontario any longer,” Trump said on his Truth Social platform.
This is not the first time Trump has attempted a nationalistic renaming of a geographical feature. In January 2025 Trump issued an executive order to refer to the Gulf of Mexico as the “Gulf of America”.
Mexico argued the US cannot legally change the Gulf’s name because the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea dictates that an individual country’s sovereign territory only extends up to 12 nautical miles out from the coastline.
Lake Ontario with the skyline of Toronto in the distance. Photograph: RM Nunes/Alamy
A new rule proposed by the Trump administration aims to kill public notification for datacenter air pollution, public health advocates warn, and allow emission permits to be issued behind closed doors.
The datacenters are often sources of nitrogen oxide, which helps form ozone, carbon monoxide and heavy metals, among other pollutants.
The Clean Air Act requires “minor” air polluters to disclose to the public via state agencies how much pollution their proposed project will release, but the proposed new rule from Donald Trump’s Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) would dismantle that protection for datacenter proposals. Instead, it would make disclosure voluntary at state and some local officials’ discretion.
Many state political establishments support datacenters, and observers say it is unlikely most would voluntarily require big tech to disclose the information. The move is likely intended to curb criticism and public oversight of datacenters, said Joe Goffman, a former assistant administrator for the EPA’s office of air and radiation.
Without this data, communities won’t know what they’re breathing once a datacenter is built, and will have less ability to fight back in court or in public relations battles. Goffman said the Clean Air Act is supposed to offer “an ironclad promise” to give the entire US public a voice on these issues.
“The administration is basically saying: ‘You all may have thought this was an ironclad promise, but it no longer is,’” Goffman added. He co-authored comments on the proposed rule submitted by the Environmental Protection Network. The EPA just closed the public comment period, and the rule could face a legal challenge if finalized.
Trump also noted claimed today that the Iranian regime is “not paying large segments of their military while at the same time killing protesters, even when they are not protesting”.
This comes after the treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, announced “unprecedented” sanctions against countries that continue to do business with Iran.
“Our objective is to sever every economic lifeline that sustains this tyrannical regime until Tehran stands alone,” Bessent said on Monday.
While Iran’s currency, the rial, dropped to a new low on Monday, it’s unclear how the US plans to roll out new secondary sanctions to target those trading with Iran. This week, Bessent evaded reporters’ questions about a timeline or whether China – the largest importer of Iranian oil – would be targeted.
“We are level-setting with every country to tell them our expectations. We know who they are. They know who they are,” he said.
On Truth Social, however, the president shot down assertions that the US talks with Canada collapsed in part due a proposed trade deal that would have weakened French language protections.
“I would never interfere with Canadians speaking French!” he wrote. “In fact, I have never even thought of doing such a stupid thing. This lie was made up by a weak and ineffective Prime Minister in an attempt to gain political support, which he has totally lost, from the people of Quebec.”
As my colleague Leyland Cecco reports, Quebec – Canada’s predominantly French-speaking province – has long sought to protect its distinct identity, at times with laws that clashed with the federal government and the Canadian charter of rights and freedoms.
In recent years those rules have also frustrated US negotiators, who have framed them as trade irritants. Bill 96, for example, requires products sold in Quebec to have a French description and for trademarks using generic terms to be translated into French, while Bill 109 compels media services such as Netflix, Spotify and Apple to promote and prioritize French content for Quebec users.
Donald Trump is in Washington today. As of now, he doesn’t have any public events, but we will let you know if anything changes and opportunities arise for him to speak with the press.
If Ralph Norman becomes the nominee in South Carolina and goes on to win the November election, he has a reputation in the House of Representatives of putting up resistance, at least temporarily, to some Republican leadership demands, which could preview how he would operate as a senator.
Norman, 73, a longtime real estate developer, has spent nearly a decade in the US House. He mounted an unsuccessful bid for governor, finishing third in a June primary.
He has been a leading member of the right-wing House Freedom Caucus, but endorsed the more moderate Nikki Haley in her 2024 failed presidential bid.
Nonetheless, Norman supports many of Trump’s initiatives, including a nationwide tightening of requirements for casting votes throughout the US, which Democrats say would make it more difficult for eligible citizens to participate in elections. Norman has also backed Trump in opposing congressional constraints on the US war against Iran.
Ralph Norman participates in a televised debate ahead of the Republican primary runoff. Photograph: Anadolu/Getty Images
For her part, Darline Graham used a Myrtle Beach rally alongside Trump to try to recover from what has been cast as a debate misstep when she said she was not knowledgeable about national security issues, on which her late brother had expertise.
“Guilty as charged,” Graham proclaimed at the rally. Instead, she focused her remarks on her stances on domestic issues, including Trump’s immigration clampdown and anti-abortion advocacy – matters that likely are higher on South Carolina voters’ list of concerns than foreign policy.
She had never held public office until her appointment to the Senate, having previously held positions advocating for people with physical disabilities.
South Carolina, a deep red state, has overwhelmingly embraced Trump in all three of his runs for president and is not likely to play a role in the Republican-Democratic battle for the control of Congress.
Darline Graham at a news conference for her campaign. Photograph: Meg Kinnard/AP
Darline Graham and Ralph Norman head to South Carolina’s Senate runoff
Voters in South Carolina will decide whether they want to establish a Graham family dynasty as they go to the polls today in a Republican primary pitting Darline Graham against US Representative Ralph Norman.
Graham, 62, is the sister of Lindsey Graham, who died at the age of 71 on 11 July, having served in Congress for 31 years – 23 of those in the US Senate. She was appointed to finish his Senate term that expires at the beginning of January.
The primary will decide whether the current Senator Graham or Norman will be the Republican nominee in the 3 November election, facing Democrat Annie Andrews, a pediatrician, for a six-year Senate term.
Donald Trump has endorsed Graham and held a rally for her on Friday in Myrtle Beach, South Carolina, The primary election will be another in a series of tests of Trump’s sway with voters in this year’s midterm elections.
MAGA INC, a super PAC that supports Trump, has spent $827,711 (£607,000) in support of Graham, according to its filing on Monday with the Federal Election Commission.
Darline Graham and Ralph Norman participate in a televised debate ahead of the Republican primary runoff. Photograph: Anadolu/Getty Images

The Kremlin said it had no information on a US military transport plane landed at Moscow’s Vnukovo airport earlier today.
Reuters reported that data from the flight tracking service Flightradar24 showed that the large Boeing Globemaster had flown direct from Riga, in Latvia, and landed in Moscow at around 7am GMT. The news agency was unable to verify whether it carried any cargo or passengers.
The aircraft had arrived in Riga on 23 August from the US Camp Springs airbase near Washington DC, data from Flightradar24 showed.
The last direct flight of a US registered jet to Russia from Europe took place in January this year, carrying special envoys Steven Witkoff and Jared Kushner for peace talks with Vladimir Putin on Ukraine.
The Kremlin said last week that there was no information yet on another visit to Moscow by Kushner and Witkoff, as talks between the US and Russia on Ukraine have largely stalled amid the war in Iran.
USS Abraham Lincoln to dock in Thailand after record deployment
Despite reports over poor conditions on board the US Navy aircraft carrier the USS Abraham Lincoln, which will dock in Thailand next week following a period of more than 200 consecutive days of deployment, Donald Trump claimed the ship was “beautifully maintained”.
Earlier this month, the president berated Kristen Holmes, a CNN reporter, insisting that she “be quiet” and describing the reporting of poor conditions on board as fake news.
“The Lincoln has been out there for a period of time – a good period of time – but over the years, we’ve had them out there much longer,” Trump said, describing an exchange with a veteran, whom he did not name.
“He happened to be an admiral, retired. He said, ‘I’ve been on ships that are out there much longer than that, sir. And I know people on the Lincoln, they say it’s beautifully maintained and beautifully taken care of.’ And other people went out and they found out that to be true,” said Trump.
The US Navy aircraft carrier the USS Abraham Lincoln will dock in Thailand next week, following a prolonged deployment in the Middle East during the Iran war, a Thai official said on Tuesday.
The Lincoln, which left the Middle East on Saturday, has not make a port call in more than 200 days, setting a modern-day record for consecutive days at sea, according to Democrats, amid reports of concerns about mental health and deteriorating conditions aboard.
The ship, which has roughly 5,000 sailors and marines aboard, will be in Thailand for “rest and recreation after their long sea journey,” the official said, asking not to be named. A Thai Navy spokesperson did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
In an interview last week, the wife of a sailor onboard the USS Lincoln told the Guardian as the deployment has stretched on and on, she has noticed a change in her husband’s messages. “There’s less hope in the way he talks and less positive things that he has to say,” she said.
“He’s just exhausted,” she added. “It’s a long, long deployment and it takes a toll.”
Reports from families of crew members published in the Navy Times and Stars and Stripes military newspapers described food and water shortages, disrupted mail services, plumbing problems, low morale and worsening mental health, prompting Democratic lawmakers to demand answers from the Pentagon.
Republican and Democratic politicians have called on the Trump administration to bar American citizens and businesses from supporting Chinese and Russian civilian intelligence and security agencies, Reuters reports.
Congress approved a law in 2018 banning Americans from providing support to foreign military intelligence agencies but leaving the door open to such aid for similar civilian-led organisations. In 2019, Reuters revealed the United Arab Emirates had hired over a dozen former US intelligence operatives to hack dissidents, journalists, and Americans.
Rules implementing a 2022 congressional measure to bolster controls have not yet been finalised, leaving “glaring loopholes that harm US national security and foreign policy interests,” Democratic Senator Ron Wyden and Republican John Cornyn wrote in a letter addressed to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick.
Canada said it will announce its response to Donald Trump’s new tariffs, as the neighbours that used to be close allies spiral into a trade war.
Canadian PM Mark Carney said on Monday that while American negotiators saw the French language in Canada as an “irritant … in Quebec, these are rights,” days after receiving widespread praise from political leaders for rejecting a US trade proposal that many perceived as weakening the country’s Francophone culture.
The prime minister’s remarks came hours after Trump showed little interest in retreating from the spat, posting on social media that Canada had been “ripping off the United States of America for years” and threatening a swath of new, economically devastating tariffs on cars and trucks.
Carney instructed his negotiators to walk away from trade talks last week. Tariffs on an array of Canadian products took effect over the weekend, affecting around 5% of Canada’s exports to the US, and Canada said it will retaliate in early September.
Quebec’s premier, Christine Fréchette, said Carney had made the right decision in walking away from talks that looked to cross a “red line” for Francophones. On Monday, Trump’s top trade representative, Jamieson Greer, called reports that French language protections were up for debate a “a funny fake story”.
“That is not true,” Greer told CNBC. “I like the Quebecois and I like that they speak French.”
Also in US news today:
Darline Graham and Ralph Norman face South Carolina voters yet again in a special Republican primary runoff to replace the late Lindsey Graham in the Senate, one month after his sudden death. Darline Graham is a political newcomer now serving as interim replacement for her brother. She has struggled to define herself to voters who routinely backed her brother. Norman has stressed his experience servicing in state and federal office.
Tulsa businessman Mike Mazzei is hoping to win a hotly contested Republican primary runoff for Oklahoma governor against state Attorney General Gentner Drummond. Trump has endorsed Mazzei and sharply attacked Drummond. The winner will face Oklahoma House Minority Leader Cyndi Munson in a vote to be governor of the deeply conservative state.
The Supreme Court is siding with the Trump administration in a case over Trump’s executive order restricting mail-in voting, though it remains unclear how much can be implemented before the fast-approaching midterm elections. The US Postal Service laid out its plan for implementing the order last week, but time is running short to impose major changes.
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Trump had congratulated Ukraine on its independence day. The message that Zelenskyy shared on X read: “Let us seize this moment to end the conflict and build a durable, lasting peace that unleashes the tremendous potential of Ukraine for generations to come.” Zelenskyy said on Sunday that his country is receiving substantially fewer Patriot defence systems, even as Russian ballistic attacks are increasing.
summary: Donald Trump claimed on social media that the United States is considering renaming Lake Ontario to Lake America amid an escalating trade war with Canada. Meanwhile, the Trump administration proposed a new rule that would eliminate public notification requirements for datacenter air pollution. Additionally, South Carolina voters are heading to the polls in a Republican primary runoff for the US Senate featuring Darline Graham and Representative Ralph Norman.
key_points: Donald Trump stated the US might rename Lake Ontario to Lake America due to a trade dispute with Canada.
A proposed EPA rule would dismantle public disclosure requirements for minor air polluters like datacenters.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced unprecedented sanctions aimed at severing economic lifelines to Iran.
South Carolina voters are deciding between Darline Graham and Ralph Norman in a Republican primary Senate runoff.
The US aircraft carrier USS Abraham Lincoln is set to dock in Thailand after over 200 consecutive days at sea.

title: China warns it will safeguard its interests after US widens sanctions against Iran
author: Ian Aikman
content:
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent says US will "tighten the noose" around Iranian revenue sources
- Published
China has vowed to protect its interests after the US announced plans to widen economic sanctions against Iran and its trading partners, which include Beijing.
Foreign ministry spokesman Lin Jian said China was firmly opposed to what it called "illegal unilateral sanctions" and would take "all necessary measures" to safeguard its rights.
This came after US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced the new measures on Monday, warning any nation financially partnering with Iran would be isolated.
China is the biggest buyer of Iranian oil, although the trade has declined under the US blockade of Iran's ports.
Lin said: "Cooperation between China and Iran has always been conducted within the framework of international law and should not be interfered with or disrupted."
Bessent described the plans for sanctions as "the single greatest financial offensive ever" against Iran, warning banks and businesses would share in Iran's isolation if they refused to cut ties with the country.
He declined to focus on specific nations, but said US President Donald Trump would be phoning world leaders "with specific requests to cease their interactions with the regime".
However, responding to a question about Chinese banks, Bessent said he wanted to make clear "no one was above the reach of US sanctions".
The announcement comes ahead of planned talks between Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping next month.
Washington is likely to be wary of potential retaliation from Beijing, which processes the majority of the world's rare earths and other critical minerals, crucial in the manufacture of many high-tech products.
Beijing has already tightened export controls on rare earths as part of previous trade negotiations with the US.
China's response followed Iranian Economy Minister Ali Madanizadeh saying Tehran was "fully prepared" for the wider sanctions, which he said would lead to "another defeat" for the US.
"The government is and was ready and has a two-year plan to manage these events," he told state television.
"We also have our own tools and know how to play the game," he said, adding Tehran had been "waiting for these plans for a long time".
The US has dubbed its latest sanctions "Operation Economic Outcast" and described them as an "economic D-Day" against Iran.
It comes almost six months after the start of the Iran war.
The conflict has since led to hikes in oil prices worldwide, with Tehran effectively blocking exports through the Strait of Hormuz - a waterway vital to the global economy. The US has also slowed traffic via its own naval blockade.
Recent attempts to end the conflict via diplomacy have failed, and a 60-day ceasefire formally expired last week with no sign of a settlement.
With the announcement of new sanctions, the US treasury secretary claimed America was "no longer managing the Iranian threat, we are ending it".
Iran is already under heavy sanctions from the US, but Bessent said these go further.
He said the Treasury had mapped financial channels, facilitators and networks used by Iran to evade sanctions to trade oil, imposing sanctions on almost 60 entities, individuals and vessels.
But analysts had cast doubt on the latest measures even before China's response.
David Oxley, chief climate and commodities economist at Capital Economics, told the BBC the direct impact on Iran's energy revenues would be "somewhat of a damp squib".
"We suspect that the new package will have only a limited direct impact on Iranian energy flows in the short term," he added.
This is partly due to the fact roughly 90% of Iran's oil goes to China, he said, "which has not recognised US sanctions in the past and is unlikely to be cowed this time either".
Ali Vaez, deputy director of the Middle East and North Africa Program at the International Crisis Group, said: "Generally, the Chinese are against unilateral sanctions. They would comply with multilateral or international sanctions, but unilateral sanctions just imposed by the US - they have always seen that as illegitimate."
And although Iran's neighbours like Pakistan, Turkey and Iraq want to maintain good relationships with the US, they "can't really afford to cut off ties with Iran", Vaez told BBC Radio 4's Today programme.
He said putting economic pressure on Tehran "doesn't work" because the Iranian regime is willing to "absorb any pain" and pass it onto the people.
Other trade partners that could be affected by the US announcement include India and Russia, who have not yet responded.
summary: China has vowed to protect its interests after US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced a wide-ranging package of new economic sanctions targeting Iran and its trading partners. Bessent warned that nations, banks, and businesses financially partnering with Iran will face isolation. In response, Beijing condemned the unilateral sanctions, while Iranian officials stated Tehran is fully prepared for the measures.
key_points: US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced new sanctions dubbed 'Operation Economic Outcast' to target Iranian revenue sources and its financial partners.
China, the largest buyer of Iranian oil, stated it firmly opposes unilateral sanctions and will take all necessary measures to safeguard its rights.
Iran's economy minister stated that Tehran is fully prepared for the wider sanctions and possesses a two-year plan to manage them.
The new US measures come ahead of planned talks between President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping next month.
Analysts have expressed doubt over the short-term impact of the sanctions, noting that China and other regional partners are unlikely to completely cut ties with Iran.

title: US removes Syria from ‘state sponsor of terrorism’ list
author: Al Jazeera Staff
content:
![ANKARA, TURKEY - JULY 08: U.S. President Donald Trump (R) meets with Ahmed al-Sharaa, President of Syria (L) for bilateral talks at Beştepe Presidential Compound during the NATO Summit on July 08, 2026 in Ankara, Turkey. Leaders from NATO's 32 countries, plus NATO allies like Ukraine, gathered in the Turkish capital to discuss a range of issues involving spending targets, defense industrial production, and support for Ukraine, among other topics. (Photo by Win McNamee/Getty Images)](https://www.aljazeera.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/getty_6a4eb0a820-1783541928.jpg?resize=730%2C410&quality=80)
Removing sanctions gives Syria's economy a chance to breathe: Analysis
The United States has removed Syria from its list of “State Sponsors of Terrorism”, a decision Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa hailed as “historic” and said would help the country’s recovery after 14 years of civil war.
The removal on Monday took effect after a 45-day congressional review period, triggered when US President Donald Trump formally notified Congress on July 8 of his intention to rescind the decades-old designation.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4US pressure on Israel needed for peace in Syria
- list 2 of 4Envoy says Israel did not give the US notice before strikes on Syrian base
- list 3 of 4Syria’s foreign minister says door open for diplomacy with Israel
- list 4 of 4US envoy Tom Barrack retracts comment that Syria’s Golan is occupied
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said in a statement that the action was “taken in recognition of the positive actions taken and further commitments” by al-Sharaa to “fully distance Syria from acts of international terrorism”.
Al-Sharaa welcomed the decision in a statement on X.
He thanked Trump and said Syria was tearing a “page from its painful past, in order to launch itself into the realm of development, reconstruction, and building”.
Syria had been on the list since 1979, when Washington accused the government of former President Hafez al-Assad of supporting armed groups. The designation remained throughout the rule of his son, Bashar al-Assad, who was toppled by rebels led by al-Sharaa in December 2024.
The designation carries restrictions on US foreign assistance, defence exports and sales, certain dual-use items (which can have civilian and military applications) and financial transactions. It had remained a major deterrent for banks and investors even after Washington dismantled its broader sanctions programme on Syria.
Iran, Russia influence
Al Jazeera’s Kimberly Halkett, reporting from Washington, DC, said the US move ends five decades of Syria’s isolation.
“Only Cuba, Iran, and North Korea remain on that list. This will open up an opportunity for international legitimacy – something al-Sharaa’s government has been seeking. But it also paves the way for commercial investment, not only in the form of US financial assistance, but also defence sales,” she said.
“Strategically, there’s another goal of the United States in all of this: to try to pull Syria away from the clutches of both Iran and Russia, and end the formal pariah status Syria has previously found itself in,” she added.
Monday’s announcement also revoked the designation of al-Nusrah Front – the group formerly led by al-Sharaa, also known as Hayat Tahrir al-Sham (HTS) – as a global “terrorist” organisation. HTS was once al-Qaeda’s official branch in Syria.
It represents a further vote of confidence in al-Sharaa, who has launched what many experts have described as a charm offensive aimed at Western powers, including meetings with Trump and French President Emmanuel Macron.
“Today’s action will help foster additional investment in Syria to promote political and economic stability,” US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in a statement, adding that it is “in line with President Trump’s promise to deliver sanctions relief to Syria”.
‘A new chapter’
Syria’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs said the US action “represents an important shift that opens a new chapter in international relations with Syria”. It said the move “will contribute to supporting economic recovery efforts and creating suitable conditions for reconstruction and enhancing stability in Syria and the region”.
The governor of Syria’s central bank, Safwat Raslan, said on X that this is “a historic step that restores the country to its natural place in the global economic system”. He added that the bank is “working to build a modern and reliable financial system”.
Syrian Finance Minister Mohammed Barnieh, meanwhile, described Washington’s move as “a major and historic success for Syrian diplomacy”, according to the country’s official news agency SANA.
It “opens a major and long-awaited door to strengthening Syria’s integration into the global economic and financial system, attracting investment and modern technologies, and supporting development opportunities”, he said.
The US envoy to Syria, Tom Barrack, also hailed the move.
He called the end of the designation a “decisive step in Syria’s remarkable journey from isolation to partnership, and from a source of terrorism to a committed partner in the global fight against it”.
summary: The United States has removed Syria from its "State Sponsors of Terrorism" list following a 45-day congressional review period. Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa hailed the historic decision, which aims to aid the country's economic recovery and reconstruction after 14 years of civil war. US officials stated the move recognizes Syria's steps to distance itself from international terrorism and seeks to pull the nation away from Iranian and Russian influence.
key_points: The US removed Syria from the state sponsor of terrorism list after a 45-day congressional review following President Donald Trump's notification.
Syria had been on the list since 1979 under the government of Hafez al-Assad and remained there through Bashar al-Assad's rule until rebels led by Ahmed al-Sharaa toppled him in December 2024.
The US also revoked the designation of the al-Nusrah Front, the group formerly led by al-Sharaa, as a global terrorist organisation.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio stated the action recognizes al-Sharaa's commitments to fully distance Syria from international terrorism.
The policy shift lifts restrictions on US foreign assistance, defence sales, and financial transactions to help foster economic stability and reconstruction in Syria.

title: Natalie Harp spotted in Trump’s VIP box after storm over her deeply personal letters
author: Ariana Baio
content:
Natalie Harp spotted in Trump’s VIP box after storm over her deeply personal letters
- President Donald Trump and First Lady Melania Trump attended the inaugural Freedom 250 Grand Prix IndyCar race on the streets of Washington, D.C.
- Executive assistant Natalie Harp watched the race from the president's viewing box following recent public scrutiny regarding her close working relationship with Trump.

- American driver Kyle Kirkwood won the race after navigating a challenging circuit around the Capitol that included a notable two-car crash.

title: US plans to revoke 200,000 visas of asylum seekers
author: Evelyn Ann-Marie Dom
content:
The move is the latest in the Trump administration's crackdown on immigration. If it happens, the move would mark the largest single mass revocation of visas in US history.
The Trump administration said on Monday it is planning to revoke business and tourism visas of 200,000 foreigners who have applied for or are currently seeking asylum in the United States.
Unless challenges or revised, the move would mark the largest single mass revocation of visas in US history.
“We are coordinating with DHS to identify and revoke the nonimmigrant visas of foreigners who have come to the United States claiming to be short-term visitors, but then file for asylum to stay here permanently,” State Department spokesman Tommy Pigott said.
He did not comment on the exact number of visas that would be revoked, claiming that "the number of revocations remains dynamic and will be done on a rolling basis".
In the coming weeks, the State Department is expected to announce the revocation of B1 and B2 visas issued between 2016 and 2026 for those that have sought or are currently seeking asylum, according to documents obtained by press agency The Associated Press and two US officials that spoke on condition of anonymity.
B1 visas are typically issued for business trips and B2 visas for tourism, family visits and medical care. Current applicants for both categories are asked to confirm that they are not seeking asylum in the US and provide proof that they intend to return to their home countries.
The revocation of the visa would not immediately result in the deportation of the individual, the officials clarified, but those with pending asylum cases would lose their status as business or tourism travellers.
The move is the latest in the Trump administration’s broader immigration crackdown, which has intensified since President Donald Trump returned to office for his second term.
The administration has already tightened restrictions on visa applicants, including requiring applicants to provide their social media histories, imposing expensive bonds before visas can be processed, and complete visa bans on citizens of certain countries.
On Friday, a judge struck down a Trump administration policy implemented earlier this year that suspended the visa issuance of immigrant visas from 75 countries.
US District Judge Jeannette Vargas, who was appointed by former President Joe Biden, said the policy was "contrary to law and in excess of statutory authority," arguing that it undermines Congress's requirement that consular officers are at the forefront of making visa decisions.
summary: The Trump administration is planning to revoke the business and tourism visas of approximately 200,000 foreigners who have applied for or are seeking asylum in the United States. State Department officials stated that the revocations will occur on a rolling basis and represent the latest action in a broader immigration crackdown. While affected individuals would lose their visitor status, officials clarified that the action would not immediately result in deportation.
key_points: The administration plans to revoke B1 and B2 visas issued between 2016 and 2026 for individuals seeking asylum.
The move would mark the largest single mass revocation of visas in US history if unhindered.
Revocation does not immediately trigger deportation, but individuals will lose their business or tourism traveler status.
A federal judge recently struck down a separate Trump administration policy that suspended immigrant visa issuances from 75 countries.

title: Israeli crime boss shot dead at point-blank range
author: Melanie Swan
content:
An Israeli mafia boss has been shot dead in public at point-blank range.
Yanis Yushvaev, 40, was killed as he left a petrol station near Caesarea on Sunday.
The married father of three was considered one of Israel’s most dangerous criminals, with his death coming as the country grapples with a growing organised crime crisis.
CCTV footage showed the gunman walking up a small flight of steps to a door, as two men came out of it and walked past him. Yushvaev was then seen coming out of the door and walking down the stairs.
After the men had walked past the gunman and were facing the other way, he turned and shot Yushvaev in the back of the head. The mafia boss then tumbled down the stairs as the gunman fled on foot.
Police described Yushvaev as the head of a crime group associated with Israel’s Jewish Caucasus community.
He had evaded conviction for years as police repeatedly failed to gather sufficient evidence despite his own alleged involvement in shootings, grenade attacks and vehicle arson.
Restaurants targeted in crime family feud
There is growing concern that Israel’s underworld wars are spilling into everyday public spaces.
In recent weeks, branches of Japanika, a popular sushi restaurant chain, have been targeted with grenades, gunfire and attempted arson in attacks police have linked to an escalating feud between the Mosli (Jewish) and Jarushi (Arab) crime families.
Thirteen attacks were reported in the space of several days, including gunfire at a restaurant in Herzliya and a suspected grenade attack that caused a fire at a branch in Netanya.
The attacks prompted the US embassy in Jerusalem to issue a security warning to Americans in Israel about the threat from organised crime in Tel Aviv, Jaffa and Herzliya.
Murders are also on the rise. There were 309 murders recorded in Israel in 2025, up from 148 in 2022, an increase of 109 per cent.
Of those killed in 2025, 241 were Arab-Israelis, and 47 were Jewish, according to police figures.
But Sunday’s killing stands as a reminder that Israel’s organised crime problem is not confined to its Arab minority.
Much of the blame has fallen on Itamar Ben-Gvir, the national security minister, who took responsibility for the police at the end of 2022. He has denied accusations that he is letting the phenomenon spiral by treating the bloodshed as an internal Arab problem.
summary: Israeli mafia boss Yanis Yushvaev, 40, was shot dead at point-blank range outside a petrol station near Caesarea. Yushvaev, considered one of Israel's most dangerous criminals, was killed amid a growing organized crime crisis and rising murder rates in the country. The incident highlights concerns that underworld violence is spilling into public spaces and is not confined to the Arab minority.
key_points: Israeli mafia boss Yanis Yushvaev was killed at point-blank range outside a petrol station near Caesarea.
CCTV footage captured the gunman shooting Yushvaev in the back of the head before fleeing on foot.
Israel is experiencing a surge in murders, rising from 148 in 2022 to 309 in 2025.
Organized crime feuds have recently targeted public spaces and restaurant chains like Japanika with grenades and gunfire.
National security minister Itamar Ben-Gvir has faced accusations of letting crime spiral by treating bloodshed as an internal Arab problem.

title: Canada walked away from Trump. Could the EU ever do the same?
author: Jorge Liboreiro; Peggy Corlin
content:
Canada's Mark Carney has shown the EU what walking away from Trump could look like. But would Brussels dare call out the US president and reject his demands that allies play by his rules? For Europe, it's complicated.
Mark Carney said enough.
In a stunning decision, the Canadian prime minister has walked away from trade negotiations with the United States, his country's one-time closest ally. While the economic ramifications remain uncertain and could be severe, the former central banker has made clear that sovereignty is not a price Canada is willing to pay.
Carney denounced Washington's proposed terms as a "bad deal" that would have infringed on Canada's use of the French language, which is constitutionally protected, and its ability to sign trade deals with other nations.
"You're at war when you're attacked, and we got attacked," Carney said, promising to retaliate "dollar for dollar" against his neighbour.
The fallout is set to be painful: steep tariffs on $20 billion in Canadian goods and roughly 87,000 direct and indirect jobs put at risk, according to initial estimates.
And it could soon get worse. US President Donald Trump has already announced a new round of tariffs against Canada, fuelling the cycle of retaliation.
The spectacular fallout has drawn parallels with the European Union, which has also been on the receiving end of the White House's ever-expansive demands and negotiating tactics from a Trump administration fixated on trade deficits and determined to use every weapon to put America first, even before friends.
For over a year, Brussels has been struggling to stave off American pressure to dismantle environmental, sustainability and digital regulations, while trying to keep alive the lopsided EU-US trade deal struck last year in Turnberry, Scotland.
In July, Trump vowed that the EU would pay a "very big price" after the European Commission imposed an €890 million fine on Google for alleged self-preferencing practices and unfair treatment of app developers.
"We anticipate a substantial TARIFF to be placed on them at the earliest possible moment," Trump said. (The duty is yet to be introduced.)
As Brussels and Washington continue to negotiate tariff relief, particularly on steel and aluminium, a new question arises: Could the EU ever walk away?
Yes, it could walk away
The main reason the EU could be tempted into pulling a Carney-like move is its determination to protect its right to regulate and enforce rules within its jurisdiction, which Brussels sees as an absolute red line.
Europeans believe they have made more than enough concessions to placate Trump, most notably a 15% tariff on EU goods, and refuse to bend any further. Amending laws on Washington's whim would be tantamount to capitulation.
EU diplomats note that Trump backing down from a failed bid over Greenland and his decision to unilaterally launch a war against Iran, roiling energy markets along the way, have strengthened the collective resolve to speak up and push back.
Another reason that could embolden the EU to walk away is its vast size as the world's second-largest economy. The 27-member bloc's GDP is €18.8 trillion compared to Canada's $2.32 trillion (€1.99 trillion), making it almost ten times larger.
Last year, EU-US trade (goods and services) reached €1.77 billion, double the $872.3 billion (€748 billion) in Canada-US trade. Both Canada and the EU have a long-standing goods surplus and a services deficit with the US.
What changes is the dependency. Due to its geographic location, Canada is structurally reliant on the American market: Canada exports about 75% of its goods to the US. For the EU, whose trade links are much more diversified, the share falls to 21%.
This, in principle, gives the EU greater leverage and a stronger cushion to weather a trade war with the US should it ever feel it necessary to go down that road.
During the negotiations that preceded the Turnberry deal, the European Commission prepared a list of €93 billion worth of American goods to be targeted in a hypothetical tit-for-tat. The list, which remains valid, would be the first line of defence.
EU officials have also raised the prospect of triggering the Anti-Coercion Instrument (ACI), which allows countermeasures beyond traditional tariffs, such as excluding foreign companies from public tenders or partially suspending IP rights protection.
The instrument gained new significance when Trump doubled down on his threats against Greenland and the bloc's green and digital regulations. Both cases were seen as textbook examples of coercion for political aims.
"If Washington follows through with new tariffs over European digital taxes or regulation, it would very much reopen Turnberry and put Europe in a similar position to Canada's. European governments could well conclude that there is no stable deal to preserve and walking away is the better tactical play," Tobias Gehrke, a senior policy fellow at the European Council on Foreign Relations, told Euronews.
But the reaction would be moulded not just by the US but also by China, Gehrke noted. Trade tensions between the EU and China have soared ahead of an October deadline.
"There is a growing view in Europe that China represents the more systemic economic security challenge, and few want to fight simultaneous trade wars with Washington and Beijing," he said. "If the Trump administration pressures Europe precisely when Brussels is trying to manage a confrontation with China, Washington may calculate that Europe has limited escalation options."
No, it could not walk away
Though the EU has strong arguments and tools at its disposal to walk away, it is far from clear whether it could muster Carney's courage to do so.
Since Trump unveiled his sweeping tariffs, the 27 member states have scrambled to close ranks behind the European Commission, which negotiates on their behalf.
Some, including France, Spain and the Nordic countries, urged Brussels to stand firm and retaliate against unfair terms. Others, including Germany, Italy and Ireland, publicly pushed for a compromise, whatever the cost, to avoid a damaging all-out confrontation.
The cacophony and competing national interests tied the Commission's hands and ultimately produced a deal that satisfied no one. The EU still lacks a common strategy for dealing with Trump — a weakness the White House has sought to exploit.
While US threats on key issues like Greenland have indeed brought EU member states closer, and even ideologically aligned leaders like Italy's Giorgia Meloni have clashed with the US president, the fact that the Anti-Coercion Instrument has never been triggered illustrates just how difficult it is for member states to reach consensus and accept the economic pain that would follow an all-out confrontation with Washington.
By contrast, Carney rallied Canada behind him.
Following the collapse of the talks, Canada's provinces swiftly backed Carney. Ontario Premier Doug Ford, whose manufacturing sector stands to lose from the clash, expressed "full support for a strong response – tariff for tariff, dollar for dollar".
A new pollshows that 76% of Canadians believe Carney made the right call.
For the Canadian prime minister, picking a fight with Trump makes sense politically as it builds on the widespread antipathy that Canadians feel towards the US president, who has repeatedly floated the idea of making Canada the 51st US state.
There is another pivotal factor that could make the EU think twice: Ukraine.
Brussels has acknowledged that the EU-US trade deal was partly driven by a desire to keep Trump engaged in efforts to end Russia's war. The US president's stance on the conflict has shifted dramatically, fuelling anxiety among Europeans who know they cannot replace US intelligence or American-made air defence systems.
"It's not only about the trade. It's about security. It is about Ukraine. It is about current geopolitical volatility," European Commissioner for Trade Maroš Šefčovič said last year. "I believe from now on, we can go only for the better."
Although Canada is a staunch supporter of Ukraine, its role in the conflict is limited.
A European walk-out, by contrast, could give Trump a convenient excuse to retaliate by fully disengaging from Ukraine. (Some officials and diplomats in Brussels believe Trump has already done so, for all intents and purposes.)
"The Turnberry agreement is not a great deal. It's not a balanced deal. But it did not imply any compromise on the sovereignty of the European Union. There's no element that compromises the capacity of the European Union to regulate on digital, on climate, and so on," Ignacio García Bercero, a senior fellow at Bruegel, told Euronews.
Retaliation is also more complicated for the EU than for Canada, he added.
"Canada is a federal state and can impose countermeasures without securing the approval of its provinces," García Bercero said. "The EU is not a federal state, meaning retaliatory measures require a qualified majority of member states. So far, European capitals have shown little appetite for – or tolerance of – a trade war the Canadian way."
summary: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has walked away from trade negotiations with the United States after rejecting Washington's demands, prompting questions over whether the European Union could take a similar stance against the Trump administration. While the EU possesses a much larger economy, diversified trade, and potential countermeasures like the Anti-Coercion Instrument, internal divisions among member states, the risk of a simultaneous trade war with China, and security concerns regarding Ukraine complicate any potential walkout. Unlike Canada's unified federal response, the EU requires consensus among 27 nations, making a decisive break with the US significantly more difficult to achieve.
key_points: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney halted trade talks with the US, refusing to compromise on Canadian sovereignty and French-language protections.
The EU's economy is nearly ten times larger than Canada's, and its trade links are more diversified, with only 21% of its goods exported to the US compared to Canada's 75%.
EU member states remain divided between those urging a strong retaliation against unfair US terms and those prioritizing compromise to avoid an all-out confrontation.
Security concerns, particularly regarding Ukraine and the risk of US disengagement, provide a powerful deterrent against the EU walking away from trade agreements.
Unlike Canada, the EU is not a federal state and requires a qualified majority of member states to enact retaliatory measures, hindering a swift and unified response.

title: Iran-US war live: Trump unveils ‘economic D-Day’ sanctions
author: Alisha Rahaman Sarkar; Brendan Rascius; Bryony Gooch
content:
Iran has vowed retaliation against the US after president Donald Trump unveiled his “economic D-Day” sanctions against Tehran.
Iranian economy minister Ali Madanizadeh claimed Tehran was “fully prepared for the US sanctions”. “Our defence is no longer so defensive; the enemies should wait for an attack,” he told state media.
US defence secretary Pete Hegseth said the pivot to economic measures did not mean American strikes against Iran were off the table, saying that "by no means are we foreclosing using kinetic strikes anywhere in the Strait of Hormuz or around Iran”.
It comes after US treasury secretary Scott Bessent vowed to “tighten the noose” with fresh secondary sanctions on Tehran's trade partners, declaring that “no nation should expect to enjoy the rewards of our system while working with a regime that seeks to destroy it”.He said that an unnamed financial institution could expect to be sanctioned by the end of this week.
The Trump administration is turning up the economic pressure on Iran as the conflict drags on for nearly six months and reports say that the US military’s weapons stockpile is dwindling. President Trump has refuted the reporting, saying his country has ‘massive amounts of ‘munitions’”.
US public support for Iran war falls, reveals poll
US public approval of the war with Iran fell to its lowest level since the conflict's early days, helping to hold president Donald Trump's popularity at a record low, according to a Reuters/Ipsos poll.
The four-day poll showed just 31 per cent of Americans support US military action against Iran, down from 37 per cent in a March Reuters/Ipsos poll and 34 per cent earlier this month.
The decline was driven by fewer self-identified Republicans backing the conflict. Some 69 per cent of Republican respondents support the war, compared with 77 per cent in March.
Watch: Hegseth refuses to rule out US strikes against Iran
Pakistan and Iran made 'significant progress' in talks on conflict
Pakistan and Iran made "significant progress" in talks that focused on the US-Israeli war on Iran and a path to peace, Pakistan's interior minister said following his visit to Tehran.
Talks between the two sides focused on measures to prevent further escalation, reopening of the Strait of Hormuz and an expedited termination of the conflict, a statement from the Pakistani military said about the meeting between the country's army chief, Asim Munir, and the Iranian leadership.
The two sides also exchanged views on regional peace and the way to arrive at a negotiated settlement to the dispute, the statement said.
"The Iranian President candidly shared his government's perspective and we had a very constructive exchange on the issues involved," interior minister Mohsin Naqvi, who accompanied Munir to Tehran, said in a post on X.
Pakistan army chief holds talks with Iran
Pakistan's army chief Asim Munir held discussions with Iran that were focussed on measures including the prevention of a further escalation of the conflict and the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz, the Pakistani military said today.
Munir discussed regional peace and ways to reach a negotiated settlement to disputes, the statement ad
Netanyahu claims Iran tried to kill one of his sons
Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu has claimed that Iran tried to kill one of his sons.
However, he did not provide any details of the alleged assassination plot.
"As for my sons. Here, I think there is something quite unbelievable, yes. Iran targeted one of my sons. Iran tried to kill, to murder one of my sons," Netanyahu told Israel's Channel 14.
It was not immediately clear which of his sons he was referring to. Netanyahu's elder son, Yair, lives in Miami.
Iran vows heavy blows against US sanctions
Iran promised to retaliate against expanded US economic sanctions that the Americans said would cut off Iran's economic lifeline, with Tehran expressing confidence that major trading partners would resist Washington's pressure campaign.
Brigadier General Hossein Mohebbi, a spokesperson for Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, vowed heavy blows to the US's vital interests and energy chokepoints if Iran's infrastructure is threatened, Press TV reported.
Secretary Scott Bessent unveiled the measures yesterday but stopped short of the most punishing sanctions, saying countries that continued trading with Iran risked being forced out of the dollar-based financial system.
Oil prices steady as investors weigh impact of sanctions
Oil prices steadied this morning, after falling more than 2 per cent in the previous session, as investors assessed the impact of harsher US secondary sanctions against Iran.
Brent crude futures were down 9 cents, or 0.1 per cent, at $92.16, while US West Texas Intermediate crude was up 1 cent at $85.02 a barrel.
Both contracts fell more than 2 per cent yesterday with US crude oil falling to a one-week low on profit-taking after prices rallied over the previous two weeks.
Iran claims there is a $10 million bounty on Barron Trump
Iranian state media has claimed there is a $10 million bounty on Barron Trump, President Donald Trump’s 20-year-old son, according to a new report nearly six months into the US war with Iran.
Footage broadcast on Channel 3, which is linked to Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, was titled “Where and how should we kill Barron Trump?” Euronews reported Monday.
It reportedly displayed the location of his university, as well as Secret Service positions and escort vehicles, while claiming his whereabouts were “fully monitored.”
The clip also claimed that an unnamed young woman had evaded Secret Service protection, met privately with Barron Trump and relayed information about him to the video’s creators. It also claimed he uses Xbox to communicate privately.

Watch: US Treasury chief Scott Bessent issues stern warning to Iran's 'enablers'
Israel must face sanctions over its appalling campaigns in Gaza

summary: President Donald Trump has unveiled new "economic D-Day" sanctions against Iran, prompting Tehran to vow retaliation and claim it is fully prepared for the economic measures. Meanwhile, US public support for the war has dropped to 31 percent, and US defense officials have stated that military strikes against Iran remain an option. In parallel diplomatic efforts, Pakistani officials held talks with Iran to discuss preventing further escalation and achieving a negotiated settlement.
key_points: President Trump unveiled new sanctions targeting Iran, while US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent warned that nations trading with Tehran face secondary sanctions.
Iranian officials vowed retaliation against the US and stated that Tehran's defense is no longer purely defensive.
A Reuters/Ipsos poll revealed that US public approval for the war with Iran has fallen to 31 percent.
Pakistan and Iran made significant progress in talks focused on preventing further escalation, reopening the Strait of Hormuz, and finding a path to peace.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu claimed that Iran attempted to assassinate one of his sons.

title: France tornado: dozens injured and hundreds of homes damaged
author: Yang Tian
content:
Moment tornado tears through southern France
- Published
A tornado has torn through the French village of Pomas in the country's south-west, injuring 41 people and damaging hundreds of homes.
Local authorities said 15 people were taken to hospital, including a pregnant woman who was injured after her house collapsed on her, according to AFP news agency.
More than 120 emergency workers were deployed to the scene after winds reaching 117km/h (73mph) ripped roofs off houses and damaged an estimated 300 homes on Monday.
French authorities issued an orange alert for thunderstorms in large parts of the country's south-west, which have already been hit by power outages and transport disruptions.
![Pedestrians walk past a toppled tree after a tornado struck Pomas, southwestern France on August 24, 2026.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1008/cpsprodpb/940f/live/15a64300-a00e-11f1-9bf0-5f4ec548648d.jpg)
The extreme weather has left about 2,800 homes across 10 villages without electricity, according to officials.
Authorities in the Aude department in south-west France cancelled the third stage of the Vuelta a Espana cycling race in the area after a hailstorm in the French Pyrenees forced riders to seek shelter.
Eyewitness footage from the region captured the swirling vortex of the tornado looming in the horizon above houses and trees.
Images from the small village of Pomas, which was the hardest hit, showed uprooted trees, damaged cars and rubble from destroyed homes.
Meanwhile there were flight delays and cancellations at airports in Bordeaux, Marseille, Nice, Toulouse and north of Paris to the north, said Transport Minister Philippe Tabarot.
On average, France experiences several dozen tornadoes per year, according to the country's national weather service MÃ©tÃ©o-France.
It comes after Europe's summer of unprecedented heatwaves and wildfires, with France's south-west region among the worst affected with an area of 42,000 hectares burnt in one of the largest forest fires since World War Two.
![Damaged rooftops on buildings after a tornado struck Pomas, southwestern France on 24 August, 2006.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1024/cpsprodpb/6758/live/00056990-a018-11f1-a2b9-89b0f1145858.jpg)
  - Published3 July
 ![Elderly people with an umbrella used to protect themselves from the sun are walking through the streets of Grenoble. France, Isere, July 2, 2026. Illustrative image of the city of Grenoble during a heatwave.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1024/cpsprodpb/9f45/live/7e8ec8a0-76de-11f1-9510-1546718f668b.jpg)
- ![A satellite image showing wildfire burn marks across a large area of land in south-western France near Bordeaux](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1600/cpsprodpb/0b95/live/1efcbb90-97f4-11f1-870d-5d08c49babb2.png)
summary: A tornado struck the French village of Pomas in the country's south-west, injuring 41 people and damaging an estimated 300 homes. Winds reaching 117km/h ripped roofs off buildings, and 15 people were hospitalized, including a pregnant woman. The severe weather also caused power outages, transport disruptions, and the cancellation of a stage of the Vuelta a Espana cycling race.
key_points: A tornado hit the village of Pomas, injuring 41 people and damaging around 300 homes.
Fifteen people were taken to hospital, including a pregnant woman whose house collapsed.
Over 120 emergency workers were deployed to respond to the disaster.
About 2,800 homes across 10 villages were left without electricity.
Severe weather and hailstorms also caused transport disruptions and forced the cancellation of the Vuelta a Espana cycling race stage.

title: ‘Please get out’: Reno wildfires prompt mass evacuation
author: Daniel Bates
content:
Richard Edwards, the chief of the Truckee Meadows Fire Protection District, told CNN that the fire “continues to grow”.
“It’s over 15,000 acres and we still have zero percent containment,” he said.
The high winds had allowed the fire to travel “extremely quick and cover an area of almost six miles in less than 24 hours”, he added.
Joe Lombardo, the Nevada governor, declared a state of emergency and called the blaze an “active and rapidly evolving situation”.
Shane Akerson, a battalion chief with the Truckee Meadows Fire Protection District, said the fire was “human-caused”.
“However, that is still undergoing active investigation and we don’t have further details provided at this time,” he said.
A dangerous heatwave is sweeping seven US states with temperatures soaring as high as 118F (47.7C) in Phoenix, Arizona.
The National Weather Service’s Weather Prediction Centre issued an extreme heat warning for an area spanning from Louisiana to California.
summary: Wildfires in Reno have grown to over 15,000 acres with zero percent containment, driven by high winds that allowed the fire to move rapidly. Nevada Governor Joe Lombardo declared a state of emergency in response to the active blaze, which officials stated was human-caused and remains under investigation. Meanwhile, a dangerous heatwave with temperatures reaching up to 118F is affecting seven US states under an extreme heat warning.
key_points: The Reno wildfire has burned over 15,000 acres with zero percent containment.
Nevada Governor Joe Lombardo declared a state of emergency.
Officials stated the fire was human-caused, though the investigation is ongoing.
An extreme heat warning covers an area from Louisiana to California with temperatures reaching up to 118F.

title: US removes Syria from list of state sponsors of terrorism
author: Tom Bateman; Helen Livingstone
content:
![Two men in dark suits and red ties smile and shake hands in front of windows and American flags](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/999/cpsprodpb/0972/live/c3169dc0-a016-11f1-b109-879e35c24276.jpg)
US President Donald Trump welcomed his Syrian counterpart Ahmed al-Sharaa to the White House last year
- Published
The US has removed Syria from its list of state sponsors of terrorism after 47 years, lifting what it said was the "final major barriers" for private sector investment in the country and its reintegration into the global economy.
US Secretary Of State Marco Rubio said the move was in recognition of the Syrian government's positive actions to fully distance itself from acts of international terrorism.
The Trump administration has embraced Syria's new president, Ahmed al-Sharaa, a former militant who once had an American bounty on his head as the leader of an al-Qaeda off-shoot.
His Islamist group, Hayat Tahrir al-Sham (HTS), was also removed from the US list of global terrorist organisations.
HTS, formerly known as al-Nusra Front, was al-Qaeda's affiliate in Syria until Sharaa severed ties with the jihadist network in 2016.
In late 2024, HTS led the rebel offensive that overthrew former president Bashar al-Assad and it dominates Sharaa's transitional administration.
The US hopes to bring Syria into its orbit rather than that of Russia or China. But the risks remain significant, with Syria still far from secure and lacking representative government. It is also at the centre of growing tensions between its neighbours Israel and Turkey.
Rubio said Monday's move, which had been initially flagged in July, would give the Syrian "a path to prosperity".
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said: "Today's action will help foster additional investment in Syria to promote political and economic stability."
Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad Hassan al-Shaibani greeted the news as a "historic step", according to state-run news agency SANA.
"We will continue working to remove the effects of isolation and create an environment based on transparency, mutual interests and respect," he said.
Last year, the US also revoked the designation of HTS as a Foreign Terrorist Organisation and removed Sharaa from its list of Specially Designated Global Terrorists.
Syria's removal from the US list of state sponsors of terrorism - where it had been since 1979 - leaves just three remaining: Cuba, North Korea and Iran.
The listing carries financial sanctions, restrictions on US foreign aid and defence exports and sales and can also penalise people and other countries that trade with the sanctioned state.
summary: The United States has removed Syria from its list of state sponsors of terrorism after 47 years, lifting major barriers to private sector investment and global economic reintegration. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio stated the decision recognizes Syria's efforts to distance itself from international terrorism under its new president, Ahmed al-Sharaa. The Trump administration also removed al-Sharaa's Islamist group, Hayat Tahrir al-Sham (HTS), from the US list of global terrorist organizations.
key_points: Syria was removed from the US state sponsors of terrorism list after being on it since 1979.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio cited Syria's positive actions to distance itself from international terrorism.
Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa and his group HTS were also removed from US terror lists.
The policy change aims to lift barriers to private investment and help integrate Syria into the global economy.

title: Diner's disgust at receipt telling chef to ‘burn and spit on her eggs'
author: Barney Davis
content:
![Italian restaurant in Riccione under fire after an incident involving 17 year old waiter and owner joking about the incident with another customer](https://metro.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/SEI_309360492-5734-e1787593596281.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&w=646) 
An Italian restaurant wrote, ‘This is p***ing me off. Burn [her] eggs and spit in them’ after a tourist complained they were runny.
Clara had been visiting the Victor Lab, in Romagna, Italy for breakfast with her family last week.
But when the Brazilian mum’s scrambled eggs, juice, and coffee arrived she asked her teenage server if the eggs could be ‘a little more cooked’.
He reportedly scoffed, ‘we don’t make raw eggs here’ before taking them back to the kitchen, La Voce di Cesenatico reported.
‘In the end, they arrived very soft, but I didn’t ask for them to be recooked,’ the diner, who refused to reveal her surname after getting death threats, said.
![Italian restaurant in Riccione under fire after an incident involving 17 year old waiter and owner joking about the incident with another customer](https://metro.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/SEI_309361965-9f8c.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&w=543) 
Sign up for all of the latest stories
‘I let it go because I didn’t want to argue,’ Clara said.
But when it was time to pay she noticed something peculiar with her receipt.
In Italian, it read: ‘This is pissing me off. Burn the eggs and spit in them.’
She claimed her family became ‘scared’ over the possibility of their food getting saliva seasoning.
After telling the 17-year-old waiter she understood the message, he reportedly went ‘as white as a sheet’ and tried to throw the receipt away. But Clara told him she would call the police if he did.
She went viral after posting the receipt under a scathing one-star Google review of the restaurant.
A manager then apologised under the comment saying: ‘The behavior you reported was absolutely inappropriate and in no way reflects the values, customer service, and professional standards we strive to ensure every day.’
After the altercation blew up on social media the Victor Lab seized their chance to capitalise, trying to joke on a video on their TikTok account.
![Italian restaurant in Riccione under fire after an incident involving 17 year old waiter and owner joking about the incident with another customer](https://metro.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/SEI_309360405-1efd.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&w=646) 
The owner is filmed pretending to be a demanding diner ordering a dish with added ‘spit’ in an attempt to make light of the situation.
- 
	![ABC News coverage of the Second Inauguration of Donald Trump airs Monday, January 20, 2025 on ABC. (ABC/Jose Alvarado, Jr.) Barron Trump](https://metro.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/SEI_309359472-58f9.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&w=646&h=363&crop=1)
- Drunk Brit, 30, admits pulling down underwear and 'squatting' on packed plane
- Five youngsters who died after crashing into police car pictured
- Twelve arrested after deadly A66 crash that killed seven
They even added a poll asking customers whether the 17-year-old server should be sacked.
‘Sometimes it almost makes you laugh when you watch it, but this isn’t a laughing matter.
‘It’s serious,’ said Clara, adding she had received racist threats on social media.
summary: An Italian restaurant in Romagna faced backlash after a tourist named Clara discovered an insulting note on her receipt instructing the chef to burn and spit on her eggs. Clara had asked her teenage waiter to cook her scrambled eggs a bit more, prompting the inappropriate kitchen instruction to be printed on the bill. After the incident went viral from a one-star Google review, the restaurant issued an apology and later posted a TikTok video attempting to make light of the situation.
key_points: A tourist visiting Victor Lab in Italy requested her scrambled eggs to be cooked a little more.
When receiving her bill, she found a receipt stating in Italian to burn the eggs and spit in them.
The 17-year-old waiter went pale and tried to throw away the receipt when confronted.
The restaurant management initially apologized online but later posted a mocking TikTok video about the incident.
The diner reported receiving racist death threats and social media backlash following the viral post.

title: US threatens severe sanctions against countries with economic ties to Iran
author: Julian Borger
content:
The US has threatened to impose severe sanctions against any country or entity maintaining economic ties with Iran, hoping to achieve with economic measures what military means have so far failed to do.
It is unclear, however, how far the Trump administration is prepared to go in confronting China, Iran’s biggest trading partner, which has signalled its resistance to US economic pressure to cut off links with an ally.
Iran, meanwhile, vowed retaliation against any country that took part in the US-led isolation campaign.
Launching what he called Operation Economic Outcast, the US treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, called it an unprecedented campaign and compared it with the D-day Normandy landings, a turning point in the second world war.
“Today, in that same spirit, we are launching an economic onslaught against Iran’s financial connections around the globe,” Bessent said on Monday. “Our objective is to sever every economic lifeline that sustains this tyrannical regime until Tehran stands alone.”
Asked whether sanctions would be applied to China, which bought an estimated 80% of Iran’s shipped oil last year, he replied: “We want to make clear here today that no one is above the reach of US sanctions. That if they facilitate transactions and are part of the ecosystem that turns Iranian oil into money, into repression, they will be targeted.”
Bessent said the US had identified those that continued to deal with Iran and each violator would be given a deadline to cut ties or face US sanctions. He said the deadlines imposed would depend on individual circumstances.
“Any entity that facilitates money laundering on behalf of Iran will be removed from the US dollar system,” he said. “The clock just started ticking.”
Bessent said Donald Trump was “making phone calls to world leaders with specific requests to cease their interactions with the regime”, but he did not specify whether the US president would talk to his Chinese counterpart, Xi Jinping.
China’s embassy in Washington told reporters: “Regarding the Iran issue, sanctions and pressure do not help resolve the problem. China calls on the relevant parties to take responsible actions and resolve the issue through political and diplomatic means.”
Tehran said it would retaliate against the sanctions using a range of measures. Maj Gen Ali Abdollahi, the armed forces’ chief of staff, said the retaliation could take the form of land, sea or air operations or cyber-attacks.
The announcement of secondary sanctions against Iran comes nearly six months after the the US and Israel launched an attack on Iran that killed its supreme leader Ali Khamenei. Early expectations that the regime in Tehran would collapse or agree to Washington’s demands to give up uranium enrichment and other key elements of its nuclear programme were dashed.
