But Tehran remains defiant after nearly six months of war and has brought shipping to a virtual standstill in the Strait of Hormuz, refusing to allow unauthorised oil tankers to transit a waterway that is vital for global oil shipments. The effective blockade of the strait has pushed up global oil prices.
Describing what he said were "repetitive scenarios", Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said in a video posted on Telegram: "The fact that they (US leaders) have moved on from military operations ... to bring up the same old plans shows that they are desperate."
He said Washington must speak to Iran respectfully to find "a solution based on justice and honour."
"We have never been afraid. All of their actions - whether blockades or other military moves they have made - have failed, and this new issue of theirs will fail as well," he said.
The creation of a ‘Muslim Nato’ shows Trump is losing his grip in the Middle East
After the chaos sparked by Trump and Israel’s war in Iran, experts tell Maira Butt that the Mecca Agreement between Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey could represent a new dawn in the region.
Recap: Gas prices hit their highest mark ever for mid August as Trump’s Iran war drags on
Gas prices on Wednesday hit their highest-ever price for mid-August earlier this month, according to GasBuddy.
Patrick De Haan, the head of petroleum analysis at GasBuddy, reported in a post on X that gas prices have never gone above $4 per gallon after August 12 in any year.
On Wednesday morning, the average fuel price was just over $4 per gallon. The last time fuel cost nearly that much around mid-August was in 2022 when the national average gas price was $3.98 per gallon.
You can read more below:
summary: The Trump administration is launching a massive package of economic sanctions against Iran, termed an "economic D-Day," prompting warnings from Tehran of an earthquake-like retaliation and a blockade on Persian Gulf oil routes. Iran's currency has dropped to an all-time low amid the threats, while the ongoing conflict has impacted global oil and gas prices, constrained US military resources worldwide, and caused logistical challenges for the US Navy. Iranian officials have dismissed the new financial measures as a sign of US desperation that will ultimately fail.
key_points: US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced an unprecedented package of economic sanctions against Iran, dubbed an "economic D-Day."
Iran's security chief Mohsen Rezaei threatened an earthquake-like retaliation and warned Gulf neighbors that no oil would leave the Persian Gulf if they joined the sanctions.
Iran's currency fell to an all-time low of 1.992 million per dollar ahead of the expected sanctions.

The ongoing war has disrupted US military operations, leading to the cancellation of joint exercises with South Korea and supply shortages on the USS Abraham Lincoln following attacks on a Bahrain naval base.
US gas prices hit record highs for mid-August as conflict in the region and shipping disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz drove up fuel costs.

title: Doctor warn that Trump’s weight gain poses ‘strong risk factor’
author: Ariana Baio
content:
Doctors have warned that President Donald Trump’s weight gain is “a strong risk factor” for his health after the commander-in-chief has put on 23 pounds in three years, according to a report.
Trump, a known lover of McDonald’s and Diet Coke, has long faced concerns about his overall health, including bruising on his hands and swelling of his ankles. But in the second year of his second term, doctors have warned that Trump’s weight gain needs to take priority, The Washington Post reports.
The 80-year-old president weighed approximately 238 pounds at his physical exam in May – 14 pounds more than last year and 23 pounds more than the 215 pounds he was listed at in 2023, documented when he was arrested in Georgia, the newspaper noted.
“We know that obesity is a strong risk factor for numerous health issues — as well as premature disability and death,” Dr. Scott Kahan, the director of the National Center for Weight and Wellness, told the Post. “Addressing obesity to protect the president’s health should be a priority similar to ensuring Secret Service protections for his life.”
Trump, who has also been reported to indulge in late-night snacking, has been recommended by his White House physicians to make better dietary choices and increase his exercise to lose weight.
Other medical experts have expressed similar sentiments about the president’s weight gain.
Dr. Stuart Fischer, a former emergency room doctor and current internist, told the Daily Mail in June that “Someone has got to really quietly sit down and talk with him, and say, ‘You're playing with fire.’”
“The fact that his doctors haven't gotten through to him about weight, to me, is kind of interesting,” Fischer told the outlet. “It should be concerning.”
Trump and the White House have brushed off concerns about the aging president’s mental and physical acuity, often comparing his energy levels to that of his predecessor, whom Trump nicknamed “Sleepy Joe.”
“President Trump’s sharpness, unmatched energy, relentless work ethic and historic accessibility stand in stark contrast to what we saw during the last administration when Democrats and the legacy media intentionally covered up Joe Biden’s serious mental and physical decline from the American people,” White House spokesman Davis Ingle told the Post. “President Trump is the sharpest and most accessible President in American history who is working nonstop to solve problems and deliver on his promises.”
The Independent has asked the White House for comment.
But other officials have expressed similar concerns about Trump’s weight.
Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. told podcaster Katie Miller earlier this year that Trump’s dietary habits were unhinged.
“The interesting thing about the president is that he eats really bad food, which is McDonald’s, and, you then know, candy and Diet Coke. He drinks Diet Coke at all times. He has the constitution of a deity. I don’t know how he’s alive, but he is,” Kennedy said.
The president has acknowledged his weight through jokes.
While announcing new policies to make GLP-1s more accessible in June, the president said he had not taken a weight loss drug but joked, “I probably should.”
During a July appearance on Second Lady Usha Vance’s podcast, the president compared his weight to that of former President William Howard Taft.
“He was our heaviest president, and I have to be careful because I don’t want to supersede his record,” Trump joked.
During his first term, Trump’s weight was often criticized because he weighed 243, putting him in the “obese” category for his height of 6 ft 3 in.
Trump told his physician at the time, Dr. Ronny Jackson, that he would “like to lose 10 to 15 pounds” through dieting.
Trump did appear visibly thinner after he left the White House in 2021.
summary: Doctors have warned that President Donald Trump's recent weight gain poses a significant health risk, noting he has gained 23 pounds over the past three years. Medical experts emphasize that addressing his obesity should be a high priority, though the White House has defended the president's physical and mental acuity. Trump himself has acknowledged his weight through jokes, while officials like HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. have criticized his poor dietary habits.
key_points: President Trump weighed 238 pounds during his May physical exam, marking a 23-pound increase since 2023.
Medical experts warn that obesity is a strong risk factor for various health issues, premature disability, and death.
White House physicians have recommended that Trump improve his diet and increase exercise to lose weight.
The White House dismissed health concerns by praising Trump's unmatched energy and work ethic.
HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. publicly criticized the president's poor diet, which includes McDonald's and Diet Coke.

title: Ex-cricket captains call on Pakistan to ensure 'proper medical care' for Imran Khan
author: Kelly Ng
content:
![Imran Khan wearing a black button-up shirt and speaking into a microphone, points dramatically. Behind him are other men, and a television camera](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1024/cpsprodpb/92fd/live/5223f330-9f6f-11f1-830e-359f4d9d175a.jpg)
Imran Khan, shown here in 2022, has been in jail since 2023 on corruption charges which he denies
- Published
A group of former cricket captains, including Indian batting legend Sunil Gavaskar and one of England's longest-serving skippers Sir Alastair Cook, have called on Pakistan to ensure its ex-PM Imran Khan be given proper care while in custody.
The cricketer-turned-politician has been in jail since 2023 on corruption charges which he denies.
In a letter to Pakistan's current leader Shehbaz Sharif, the 21 former skippers aired concern that Khan, 73, was allowed "only a few hours" at a hospital last week where he was examined by a state-appointed team.
Khan's party has also filed a contempt petition against the government for not giving him access to his own doctors, as ordered by the top court.
The former cricket captains laid out three demands in their letter, the first of which is that Khan be assessed by a medical board directed by Pakistan's Supreme Court â which would include his personal physicians â particularly on the reported loss of vision in his right eye.
They also urged authorities to allow weekly visits by Khan's family, as ordered by the court, "without interruptions or administrative delays".
Finally, they asked that any treatment recommended by the medical board be "provided without delay".
"Imran Khan is 73 years old and has now spent more than three years in custody," read the letter initiated by former Australian captain Greg Chappell.
"Whatever the legal and political arguments surrounding his case, the basic decency of ensuring a court-ordered medical process is actually completed is not, in our view, a controversial request."
Among the other signatories were England's Michael Atherton, Michael Brearley, Nasser Hussain, Andrew Strauss and David Gower, India's Kapil Dev and Dilip Vengsarkar, and Australia's Belinda Clark, Adam Gilchrist, Steve Waugh and Kim Hughes.
Fourteen of the former skippers had also supported an earlier appeal for "humane treatment and proper medical care" for Khan which was submitted in February.
Khan's lawyer claimed at the time that his client had 15% vision left in his right eye after prison authorities failed to take action.
The signatories of both letters had described themselves as "former colleagues and rivals who share a bond forged on the cricket field", adding that the bond "transcends the borders and disputes that too often divide countries".
Khan, who previously captained the Pakistan national cricket team, served as Pakistan's prime minister from 2018 to 2022.
He was imprisoned in August 2023 and has faced charges in more than 100 cases, ranging from leaking state secrets to selling state gifts, all of which he and his party Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf say are politically motivated.
His jailing sparked large-scale protests by supporters, which were met with a crackdown by authorities.
Pakistan's Supreme Court had on Tuesday directed the government to transfer Khan to a private hospital to be examined by physicians.
He was instead seen by doctors at a government-run hospital in Islamabad, who deemed him "medically fit", before he was moved back to prison.
summary: A group of 21 former international cricket captains has written a letter to Pakistan's Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif urging proper medical care and court-ordered access for imprisoned former leader Imran Khan. The signatories expressed concern over Khan's health, particularly a reported loss of vision in his right eye, and demanded that he be assessed by a Supreme Court-directed medical board including his personal physicians. Khan has been imprisoned since August 2023 on various charges that he and his party deny.
key_points: Twenty-one former cricket captains sent a letter to Pakistan's leader demanding proper medical care for 73-year-old Imran Khan.
The signatories demanded that Khan be examined by a medical board directed by the Supreme Court, including his personal physicians.
The letter also requested weekly family visits and the prompt delivery of any recommended medical treatment.
Khan has been in jail since 2023 on corruption and other charges which he and his party maintain are politically motivated.

title: Divorce, smartphones and control - BBC sees how Taliban run Afghanistan
author: Kawoon Khamoosh
content:
![Portrait of Governor Abdullah Sarhadi in his office in Sheberghan. He has a long grey beard and is wearing a black Afghan headdress, and is looking to the left of the camera.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/9ba8/live/e39b75b0-9d65-11f1-b109-879e35c24276.jpg)
The governor of Jawzjan province, Abdullah Sarhadi, who fought for the Taliban was held in US detention in Guantanamo Bay for several years
- Published
Governor Abdullah Sarhadi gives money to treat a boy's broken arm and hands out funds for a local mosque - then, in his office in northern Afghanistan, an astonishing exchange unfolds.
A young woman tells the grey-bearded former Taliban commander that she wants to divorce her husband, who she accuses of months of abuse and beatings.
She will not take no for an answer.
In a country where girls are banned from secondary education, the 18-year-old argues her case calmly and confidently, her face completely hidden behind a full-face veil and sunglasses.
"If there was any chance to live together, I wouldn't be hereâ¦ I have taken my decision," she says.
After trying to persuade her to avoid divorce, the governor later comments that women are "mindless" and "deficient in intellect", to laughter from the male officials, bodyguards and elders around him.
The moment gives a rare glimpse into the day-to-day realities of the Taliban's rule, five years after they swept aside the US-backed government in 2021.
Watch: Eighteen-year-old woman argues her case for a divorce, saying her "honour and dignity have already been ruined"
In that time, women have been excluded from most workplaces, banned from universities and may not travel alone or visit parks and leisure centres.
In encounters spread over two years, the BBC gained unusual access to influential figures in the extreme Islamist movement, spending time with men who once planned suicide attacks or spent years in underground hideouts, but are now officials and soldiers.
The Taliban came into power saying they had changed, but many of their policies are similar to the hard-line interpretation of Sharia - Islamic religious law - they imposed in the 1990s.
The men we met seemed to want to present themselves as reasonable, yet were not keen to discuss their past violence. And we saw moments of unease between the rulers and those they rule.
Governor Sarhadi says Tuba â not her real name â should stay in the marriage.
"Ask yourself: 'Who would marry me after I get my divorce?'" says Sarhadi. "You'll have to compromise a lot or you'll lose your dignity and honour."
"Mr Governor, my honour and dignity have already been ruined," she responds.
Her husband listens, awaiting his turn to speak.
Under Sharia, a woman requesting that her husband agrees to a divorce may have to return some or all of the money given to her by him when they married. A financial settlement is often agreed. But this woman's husband says he wants four times the amount, which her family refuses to pay.
The governor says the woman should be given her own room. He adds that officials will warn him not to beat her - "otherwise he'd be jailed".
Unsatisfied, Tuba's father later tells the BBC the family will pursue divorce through the courts, even though, under the Taliban's court system, it is very difficult for a woman to get a divorce without the husband's consent.
![Large hole in hillside in Bamiyan, Afghanistan, where a giant Buddha statue once stood, pictured in 2024. The hole is within cliffs of bare, red-tinged stone, there are trees and low-rise buildings in the foreground.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/b1a4/live/a0ebed40-9ca1-11f1-a5a0-114ca9d4a1bc.jpg)
A hole left by the destruction of one of the Buddha statues in Bamiyan - Sarhadi says he destroyed it
Sarhadi was a military commander during the Taliban's first stint in power in the 1990s. He was among thousands of insurgents who surrendered in late 2001 as a US-led coalition ousted the group.
He was held for several years in US detention in Guantanamo Bay, but eventually released.
When the Taliban regained power, he became a governor - first in the province of Bamiyan, then when we met him in late June, in Sheberghan city in Jawzjan province. He has recently become deputy commander of a military corps in the northern province of Kunduz.
Tapping on an old-style mobile with a tiny screen, he says a recent ban on smartphones for officials has slowed things down. "Before, you could send a quick messageâ¦ sending documents and getting an answer fast." If he says any more about the ban, "it will cause trouble", he adds.
But in other ways his worldview seems largely unchanged from the Taliban's position 25 years ago. Then, he was a military commander in Bamiyan, where the Taliban blew up ancient giant Buddha statues, triggering international shock and condemnation.
He initially tries to avoid our questions about the archaeological site, but eventually, he says: "I destroyed it with my own hands.
"Whatever we did and we do is in accordance with the guidance and God's lawâ¦ We smash idols rather than sell them. Why should I regret? It was God's will."
In the capital Kabul, we meet another senior Taliban figure who swapped a violent past for a role with the ruling administration.
Habibullah Badr drives us through the streets in an armoured car.
He says he was previously "responsible for the operations of suicide attackers" in Kabul.
"I know all the roads and streets very wellâ¦ we had all the information we needed about Kabul and its alleys," he says. "There were areas that needed a long time to plan."
Taliban suicide attacks killed thousands of people in Afghanistan, including many civilians.
Badr is cautious about discussing his past though, fearing it will "make people upset" and could "reopen wounds".
Asked about civilian deaths, he says the Taliban targeted US convoys and that civilians were urged to stay away from foreign bases.
Whenever I try to ask him about specific attacks that took place in civilian areas, he evades the question.
![Side shot of a man driving a car, photographed from the passenger seat. He has a full beard, glasses, black headdress with thin white stripes, a light blue top and checked waistcoat.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/8352/live/87d985f0-9d6a-11f1-a291-b542ee92de7c.jpg)
Habibullah Badr says that in the past he was involved in operations involving suicide attacks
He is currently taking time out from official roles for medical treatment, but was previously deputy head of prisons for the whole country â and ran the very jail where he was held on death row under the previous government.
Badr invites us to join him at a tribal gathering, where the head of a charitable foundation is to honour him with a medal. But things take an unexpected turn.
"Mr Badr is a pride for Afghanistan and a great fighter," says Sultan Mohammad Talaee. "But I also have a complaint. If the schools and education were open to all it would be a great work for Afghanistan. I hope this doesn't offend you."
An awkward silence follows, his audience unsure how to react. Talaee's microphone is swiftly removed.
Afterwards, he tells the BBC: "I requested for the girls' schools to reopenâ¦ seeking knowledge is an obligation for both men and women in Islam."
He adds: "There were other things I wanted to say but they didn't let me talk more."
Often those who speak out face much more severe consequences.
Women told us of the deep despair they felt over dreams thwarted by restrictions on education, and of friends jailed for protesting.
Most journalists we spoke to said they had been summoned or questioned by the Taliban's intelligence organisation, Estikhbaraat.
The BBC put some of these concerns to the Taliban government's spokesman, known as Zabihullah Mujahid.
![A man in traditional white Afghan tunic and trousers with a black waistcoat and headdress sits in a chair on a lawn. Behind him are a large fountain, neatly laid stone steps, shrubs and a tree.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1600/cpsprodpb/1d3f/live/762bff60-9d77-11f1-a7fd-5fe2fcb0be12.jpg)
Zabihullah Mujahid says women's rights and freedom of speech need to be seen "through the Sharia lens"
He has been a public face for the Taliban government since 2021. He still uses the pseudonym he went by for years during the insurgency, but he told us his real name is Tahir Shah Seddiqi - revealing it publicly for the first time.
In a lavish press centre funded by the Americans for the previous government, we ask him about the first press conference he gave there, two days after the Taliban took control of the country.
Then, he told the world the Taliban government would allow women to work and study "within our frameworks" and they would "be very active" in society. Why did they fail to keep their word?
"We are committed to women's rights, freedom of speech and other things within Sharia," he replies. "We should see everything through the Sharia lens."
Allowing women to work in offices such as his own "would lead to immoralities" and "their dignity would be undermined", he adds.
He says the issue of education for women is "under discussionsâ¦ we need a Sharia-based solution for it".
When questioned about the Taliban's crackdown on media freedom, he says: "In a society like Afghanistan we have our restrictions. We can't let media do whatever propaganda they wantâ¦ they can't broadcast against Islamic laws and rites."
![Map of Afghanistan showing Sheberghan in the north, the capital Kabul, east of the centre of the country, and Kandahar in the south](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/508/cpsprodpb/0650/live/c0eae700-9c9b-11f1-b109-879e35c24276.png)
The Taliban government sits in Kabul, but Mujahid spends a lot of time in the southern city of Kandahar, the Taliban's heartland, which some now consider the de facto capital.
We ask to meet the Taliban's supreme leader, Hibatullah Akhundzada, who is based there. He rarely appears in public and has never given a media interview - we are told it will not be possible at the moment.
Restrictions have been tightened in Kandahar since I last visited two years ago. Now men must have beards. Radio stations are not allowed to play music or broadcast women's voices, and we were not allowed to film in the city.
Two hours' drive away, along dusty roads, some of the group's most devoted former fighters showed the BBC the insurgents' old secret cave network.
Abid Lalai, a former fighter who now mans a checkpoint as part of a security force under the interior ministry, shows us the holes he fired from and the places he used to put his Quran and hang AK-47s.
![A bearded man in a traditional dark tunic and trousers, wearing a brimless hat, sits cross-legged on the bare floor of a dark cave. He is on the left of the picture and is looking at a man sitting on the right, who is holding a torch.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/37e5/live/62faabe0-9d6c-11f1-a291-b542ee92de7c.jpg)
Abid Lalai is one of many Taliban fighters who hid out in caves to evade capture under previous governments
His superior, Abdul Samad, shows us an unmarked graveyard, saying his father is buried here, killed fighting for the Taliban.
The area is one of the most deprived in a country where the UN says three in four people cannot provide for their basic needs. Samad says the local population desperately need water, roads and clinics.
"Emirate [Taliban] officials have not forgotten us," says Samad. He says the leaders may be busy with other priorities. "We are hopeful, they will look after us sometime."
Five years since the Taliban began their second stint in power, poverty, unemployment and economic instability remain pressing concerns.
Taliban figures we spoke to said they were working to tackle them, but we met other people who believe the group itself is the country's main problem.
"I'm speechless about how a group that has no understanding about life is suddenly in power," says Hoda - not her real name - a woman who protested on the streets when the Taliban first returned to power.
"Women can't accept this situation," she tells the BBC. "They might advance restrictions but it won't stay like this forever."
"I think the Taliban are scared of educated women," she adds. "That's why they restrict women. They want uneducated women so they can't raise wise men. Because that would end the Taliban."
Additional reporting by Hafizullah Maroof
summary: The BBC gained rare access to Taliban officials in Afghanistan, examining how former insurgents manage governance five years after retaking power. Interviews and observations revealed persistent hard-line policies, including severe restrictions on women's education and movement, alongside ongoing economic struggles. While officials presented themselves as reasonable, their worldviews regarding Sharia law and societal control remain largely unchanged from the 1990s.
key_points: An 18-year-old woman calmly defied local norms by demanding a divorce from an abusive husband in front of provincial governor Abdullah Sarhadi.
Sarhadi admitted to personally destroying the ancient giant Buddha statues in Bamiyan during the Taliban's first stint in power.
Habibullah Badr, a former coordinator of suicide attacks, defended past violence and previously served as deputy head of prisons.
Taliban spokesman Zabihullah Seddiqi stated that women's rights and freedom of speech must be viewed strictly through a Sharia lens.
Ordinary Afghans continue to face extreme poverty and severe restrictions on media and education under Taliban rule.

title: Scrapping of Berlin swimming day for Black children becomes latest in long list of race-linked pool rows
author: Ashifa Kassam
content:
It was meant to be an outing for Black children in Berlin and their families, offering them an exclusive afternoon at an outdoor pool set up by a local theatre.
But the plans, slated for earlier this month, had to be scrapped after they were seized on by rightwing and conservative voices to whip up outrage, leaving organisers fending off racist emails and threats.
Berlin’s Volksbühne theatre said it had extended the invitation in hopes of dismantling some of the barriers that would normally keep these children away from the pool. While other groups had similarly been invited to use pool exclusively without incident, the idea of Black children enjoying a private afternoon at a public pool proved to be controversial among some.
“Berlin is a livable, diverse, colourful and free city. So why do we need safe spaces?” a local Christian Democrat politician, Aileen Weibeler, said on social media, while the far-right Alternative für Deutschland co-leader Alice Weidel described it as “an apartheid” in which “white people are temporarily denied access”.
It was the latest in a long list of incidents linking swimming pools to racism. Across North America and Europe swimming pools have often acted as a flashpoint for wider racial tensions and exclusions.
![Other groups had similarly been invited to use pool exclusively without incident.](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/e567a90f80672df4411680d1a620b4ce405919dc/0_0_8256_5504/master/8256.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
Earlier this summer, an open-air swimming lake in the eastern German city of Halle made headlines after it refused entry to bathers who did not speak German. In the Netherlands, the Institute for Human Rights recently ruled against a pool after it was found to have singled out a Black child for an identity check.
The list of incidents spans decades. In 2013, the Swiss town of Bremgarten moved to restrict asylum seekers’ access to swimming pools. In Bulgaria, Roma have sounded the alarm about being discriminated against at public pools, while in 2022, a swimming pool in Romania was fined just over €2,000 (£1,716) for barring entry to Romani children.
![Sibiu Aqua Park in Romania, which banned Romani children from entering.](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/043e5df638824478f863f9f316c0c8f3cfcec108/0_0_3702_2304/master/3702.jpg?width=120&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
Some of the association between racism and pools most likely comes down to the intimacy of these spaces, said Jeff Wiltse, the author of Contested Waters: A Social History of Swimming Pools in America. “They’re visually, physically, and socially intimate spaces, and I think that continues to pique people’s social anxieties,” he said.
Wiltse has long studied pools in the US, recasting them as sites that reflect the wider tensions in society at any given time, from James Brock in 1964 pouring hydrochloric acid into a whites-only pool where Black men were swimming, to the Texas police officer who in 2015 pinned an unarmed Black teenager to the ground and drew his gun as he sought to break up a pool party.
![Motel manager James Brock dumps acid into a ‘whites only’ pool in Florida in 1964 after black and white demonstrators jumped in.](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/1cc3627818919db580cd0b7299d03756ed18ebfe/0_0_2964_1976/master/2964.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
In the US, “throughout much of the 20th century, swimming pools were homogenous spaces”, he said. “There was explicit racial segregation of public pools.”
In the late 1940s, as public swimming pools in the US began to be racially desegregated, private pools began to spring up, particularly in suburbs that were almost exclusively white. Many people came to see swimming pools as “a certain type of social space in which the people there are all socially similar”, said Wiltse, who advocates tackling the issue by increasing public investment in community pools that could bring together people from different ethnic and racial backgrounds.
The racialised history of pools – and its continued legacy today – has helped to give rise to a stark racial divide when it comes to swimming ability, one that has had deadly consequences. In the US, the fatal-drowning rate of Black and African American children is three times higher than that of white children.
The statistics are even worse in England, where recent data found that children from Black, Asian and minority ethnic communities are 3.5 times more likely to drown than their white counterparts. Recent figures from Sport England suggest that 95% of Black adults and 80% of Black children do not swim at all.
In 2022, Katrice Rodrigues set out to change this with the launch of Unity Swimming, a community organisation that runs weekly classes aimed at Black and Asian communities.
“People get angry at that, saying: ‘How can it be inclusive if it’s just for Black and Asian communities?’” said Rodrigues, who is also a keynote speaker on diversity in aquatics. “My thing is that we’re making the whole of swimming more inclusive by creating these safe little spaces, which lead to more people swimming, and that makes swimming, as a whole, more inclusive.”
The success of the programme has relied on Rodrigues and her team confronting the wide range of cultural barriers that keep minorities out of the pool, from having parents who are terrified of water to concerns over feeling out of place, dressing modestly or protecting Black hair.
![In 1952, 17-year-old Mamie Livingston (right) challenged racial segregation in Baltimore, Maryland, by seeking admission to a whites-only public swimming pool.](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/b9d9836e2316f20b77e19adde77f468e3a111285/0_0_1200_940/master/1200.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
Other barriers have proven more enduring. “There’s a myth and a stereotype that Black people can’t float and can’t swim,” she said. “It’s not true, but I’ve had to correct two experienced swim teachers who thought that was a thing.”
As summers become hotter across the globe, sending more people into rivers, lakes and pools in search of respite, the imperative has grown to ensure that as many people as possible know how to swim, said Rodrigues.
“It’s the only sport that’s going to save lives,” she said. “If you’ve got water safety knowledge, you could help save someone else’s life as well as your own and your whole family. So this has a knock-off effect on families, on communities and for generations.”
summary: An exclusive swimming event for Black children and their families in Berlin was cancelled after facing backlash, racist emails, and threats from conservative and right-wing figures. This incident reflects a long history of racial tensions, segregation, and discrimination at swimming pools across North America and Europe. Experts and organizers note that such exclusion and associated cultural barriers contribute to significant racial disparities in swimming ability and higher drowning rates among minority children.
key_points: A Berlin theatre scrapped an exclusive pool event for Black children following right-wing outrage and racist threats.
Swimming pools globally have frequently served as flashpoints for racial tensions, discrimination, and segregation over decades.
The physical and social intimacy of swimming pools often triggers social anxieties and reflects wider societal racial divisions.
Racial disparities in swimming ability persist, with Black and minority ethnic children facing significantly higher drowning rates than white children.
Organizers like Unity Swimming use targeted classes to overcome cultural barriers and improve water safety for minority communities.

title: Leah Stewart: Australian shark attack victim grateful for 'second chance at life'
author: Lana Lam
content:
![A woman with long blonde hair, wearing a white top and red skirt lying on a cream couch, with a baby sleeping on her chest.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/2cf2/live/1cb13550-6f6d-11f1-a190-1943df672931.jpg)
Leah Stewart was bitten by a shark at Sydney's Coogee Beach during a morning swim
- Published
An Australian woman bitten by a shark at a popular Sydney beach earlier this year says she has been given a "second chance at life" and will be making the most of it.
Leah Stewart, 35, was mauled by a shark during a morning swim at Coogee Beach in June, suffering multiple bites to her arms and legs, amid a spate of attacks in Australia.
The mother-of-one was placed in an induced coma and had several surgeries, including having one of her arms amputated.
In an online post on Monday, she thanked her supporters who have raised more than AU$550,000 (US$394,000; Â£289,000) for her, saying her recovery has been "incredibly difficult" but she is making "remarkable" progress.
"After what has been an incredibly difficult few months, I'm so happy that I've progressed enough to build some independence, and I can finally see some light after all of this," Stewart wrote, in her first comments since the attack.
"I want you to know that I feel like I've been given a second chance at life, and I'm not going to waste it."
Stewart said she had been "overwhelmed" by the support from family, friends and "even strangers", adding that the "you've inspired me to get better, not bitter".
An online fundraiser for her would now be closed, she wrote, with the money raised giving her the chance to recover at home as well as "options for further medical treatment down the road".
"I still have a long way to go, but my recovery has been remarkable, and a huge part of that is because of the absolute army of love, support, prayers and encouragement surrounding my family and I from all over the world."
There have been a spate of shark attacks in Australia this year, with four attacks over a two-day period in January, including one on a 12-year-old boy who later died from his injuries.
In May, a man was killed by a shark in Queensland while spearfishing and in Western Australia, a father-of-two died after he was attacked by a 4m (13ft) shark.
summary: Australian shark attack survivor Leah Stewart has expressed gratitude for a "second chance at life" in her first public comments since being mauled at Sydney's Coogee Beach in June. The 35-year-old mother suffered multiple bites to her arms and legs, leading to an induced coma, multiple surgeries, and the amputation of one arm. In an online post, she thanked supporters for raising over AU$550,000 and noted her remarkable progress toward independence.
key_points: Leah Stewart was attacked by a shark during a morning swim at Sydney's Coogee Beach in June.
She suffered severe injuries, resulting in multiple surgeries and the amputation of one of her arms.
Stewart thanked supporters for raising more than AU$550,000 for her recovery and medical treatment.
She stated that she feels she has been given a "second chance at life" and is making remarkable progress toward building independence.

title: Landslide at waste mound in Guinea capital kills 30, government says
author: Guardian staff reporter
content:
A landslide at a huge waste dump in Guinea’s capital has killed 30 people, the government said on Sunday, after heavy rains overnight prompted it to collapse, engulfing nearby tents and shacks.
The incident occurred less than a week after the government announced plans to close the site and relocate the waste because of the threat it posed, especially during the rainy season, which causes landslides and fatal flash floods each year in crowded, underdeveloped cities across parts of West Africa.
The landslide took place at about 2am (3am UK time) in the Gbessia commune of Conakry, according to a government statement.
The death toll was 30, with six people seriously injured and 16 more lightly injured, the statement said.
Rescue workers were using excavators and other tools to clear the site of the landslide, which witnesses said was large enough to bury an apartment building along with more precarious dwellings.
One woman, Cire Diallo, told reporters at the scene that her five children were killed. “I have lost all my children. All I can do is put my trust in God,” she said.
Guinea holds the world’s largest bauxite reserves and richest untapped iron ore deposit at Simandou, where a massive mining project was launched in November. But the west African country has poor infrastructure and widespread poverty, with 3.7 million of its 15.1 million people living on less than $4.20 a day, according to a World Bank report published in April.
On Thursday Guinea’s minister of territorial administration, Djénabou Touré Camara, announced that the government was closing the landfill because it was unsafe and said the waste was to be relocated outside Conakry.
The prime minister, Amadou Oury Bah, visited the landfill on Sunday to assess the damage and supervise the response, the government statement said, adding that people should “remain calm, show solidarity, and strictly follow the instructions of rescue services and the competent authorities”.
summary: A landslide triggered by heavy rains at a massive waste dump in Guinea's capital, Conakry, has killed 30 people and injured several others. The disaster occurred just days after the government announced plans to close and relocate the unsafe site due to seasonal risks. Rescue workers have been deployed to the area using excavators to clear the debris while officials assess the damage.
key_points: A landslide at a waste dump in Conakry killed 30 people and injured 22 others.
Heavy overnight rains caused the mound of waste to collapse and engulf nearby dwellings.
The government had announced plans less than a week prior to close and relocate the landfill due to safety hazards.
Prime Minister Amadou Oury Bah visited the site on Sunday to supervise the response and assess damage.

title: Iran war live: Tehran warns of ‘earthquake-like’ retaliation over Trump’s threats
author: Alisha Rahaman Sarkar; Nicole Wootton-Cane; Sam Rkaina
content:
Iran’s security chief Mohsen Rezaei has threatened “earthquake-like” retaliation should US president Donald Trump take any further action.
Tehran has also cautioned its Gulf neighbours against joining Donald Trump’s “economic D-Day” sanctions after the US said it would look to hit Iran’s financial interests.
Should Trump "take action, our confrontation will be like an earthquake," Rezaei said.
He added: “If the countries surrounding Iran join the Americans in their economic war, not a drop of oil will leave the Persian Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz, and we will also target other oil export routes from the Persian Gulf.”
Trump has promised to wage "Economic Warfare and Isolation on an unprecedented scale” on Iran in what he called the “toughest sanctions in history”. In response, Tehran accused Trump of threatening “economic terrorism”.
Iranian foreign ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei on Saturday said that the imminent US announcement of new economic sanctions on Iran was an "assertion of extraterritorial sovereignty over every independent member state of the United Nations".
Mariam’s final minutes: Inside the Israeli hospital strike that killed her – and the possible war crimes behind it
Journalist Mariam Abu Dagga was killed in the 25 August 2025 double-tap attack on Nasser Hospital in Gaza. Based on dozens of witness testimonies, whistleblowers and visual analysis, this is the most comprehensive reconstruction yet into the strike.

In pictures: Life in Iran continues amid uncertainty over state of war
Trump officials worked with Iran on deportation lists as tensions exploded, emails reveal
Newly disclosed emails show US immigration officials worked directly with Iranian representatives to deport Iranian nationals in 2025, even as tensions between Washington and Tehran were escalating.
The records, obtained by the National Iranian American Council and released Tuesday, detail cooperation surrounding three removal flights in September and December 2025 and January 2026 that returned more than 100 Iranians.
The emails indicate Iranian representatives requested changes to proposed passenger lists and that US officials sometimes accommodated those requests.

Trump cannot let Iran make him ‘look like a loser,’ says former Fox News personality
President Donald Trump cannot let Iran make him “look like a loser” because his legacy is tied up in the war with the Islamic Republic, a former Fox News personality says.
Political commentator Bill O’Reilly, the former host of The O’Reilly Factor, made the remark on Tuesday night as the six-month anniversary of the start of the war draws closer.
Appearing on NewsNation’s On Balance, O’Reilly began by saying that he believes the US does have a strategy going forward in the conflict with Iran.
”From what I understand, there is some kind of strategy that will involve a tougher approach on Iran,” he claimed. “I don’t know what it is. It’s top secret, classified.”

The life and light of Mariam Abu Dagga – Independent Arabia journalist killed by Israel in Gaza

Federal judge strikes down Trump’s visa ban from 75 countries including Iran
A federal judge in New York has struck down a Trump administration policy that suspended visa processing for citizens of 75 nations, including Afghanistan, Iran, Russia, and Somalia.
US District Judge Jeannette Vargas, appointed by President Joe Biden, set aside the policy Friday after ruling it "contrary to law and in excess of statutory authority."
The judge ruled Secretary of State Marco Rubio exceeded his authority in issuing the policy, which "runs afoul" of the Immigration and Nationality Act by mandating "the refusal of visas to eligible applicants without any basis in law."

Watch: JD Vance says keeping gas prices low is 'goal number one' of Iran war
The USS Lincoln has been at sea for 270-plus days. Here’s why conditions on board fell apart
The food shortages and other problems that sparked outrage over substandard conditions on the USS Abraham Lincoln stemmed from Iranian attacks that devastated a key Navy base on the island nation of Bahrain — leaving the ship to rely on supplies from an outpost about 2,200 miles away.
In recent weeks, relatives of some crew members went public with tales of skimpy, inedible meals, mouldy showers, broken toilets and sporadic laundry service on the Lincoln.
Military mother Danielle Rappa told NBC News that her son, who's serving on the ship, “describes the overall experience as a scene out of the [Fox TV show] American Horror Story, where he feels like everybody is dead but they don't know it yet.”

Meanwhile, newly disclosed emails reveal that US immigration officials cooperated with Iranian representatives in 2025 and 2026 to deport over 100 Iranian nationals. Separately, a federal judge in New York struck down a Trump administration visa ban affecting 75 countries, ruling the policy was contrary to law.

Newly released emails show US immigration officials worked with Iranian representatives on deportation lists in late 2025 and early 2026.
A federal judge struck down a Trump administration policy that suspended visa processing for citizens of 75 countries, including Iran.
Deteriorating conditions on the USS Abraham Lincoln stemmed from Iranian attacks on a key Navy base in Bahrain.

title: Iran threatens to strike US companies
author: Emily Blumenthal
content:
![An anti-Trump billboard in Tehran](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/en-us/news/2026/08/23/TELEMMGLPICT000498837562_17874456151770_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqQcMUUMOPcm1luMcbLfk8vEDps6O_qDhN5RXnYnbgjG0.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
![An anti-Trump billboard in Tehran](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/en-us/news/2026/08/23/TELEMMGLPICT000498837562_17874456151770_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqQcMUUMOPcm1luMcbLfk8vEDps6O_qDhN5RXnYnbgjG0.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
Iran has threatened to strike American businesses if Donald Trump launches his “economic D-Day” campaign to force Tehran to accept a deal to end the war.
Mohsen Rezai, the head of Iran’s national security council, also warned allies of the US that they would be considered enemies, and their interests harmed, if they joined the US president’s financial warfare.
Mr Trump said on Wednesday that Iran would face “economic warfare and isolation on an unprecedented scale”.
On Saturday, Mr Rezai insisted that the Islamic Republic had additional leverage in the war, claiming that “we have not yet attacked any American economic interests”.
He told Iranian state media: “So far, we have only targeted military bases, but if they want to impose economic sanctions on us, the US has oil and economic companies around Iran and elsewhere, and we will strike them.”
![Copies of Iranian daily newspaper Hamshahri and Jame-Jam displaying pictures of US President Donald Trump](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/en-us/news/2026/08/23/TELEMMGLPICT000499116051_17874454957380_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqK_vgMZMtToVksLIt2InIPf2y-wlPAGAdEo1iKHmOwyU.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
If Mr Trump enacts his plan “our confrontation will be like an earthquake”, Mr Rezai added.
The warning is believed to be the first time in months that Tehran has threatened to hit American and Western businesses, and the only time it has explicitly mentioned their oil companies.
The Telegraph revealed on Saturday that hackers linked to the Iranian regime had shut down a British power plant for four days in a cyber-attack.
Iran’s threat against American allies, most of which have not backed Mr Trump’s war, mirrored the US president’s warning on Wednesday that countries providing “any kind of lifeline” to Tehran would face “tremendous economic consequences”.
In a post on his Truth Social network, Mr Trump announced “the most crushing economic operation ever” against Tehran, and called on allied countries to “stand with the United States of America to isolate, and defeat, the Iran threat”.
The Telegraph reported last week that Mr Trump had decided to pivot to squeezing Iran’s economy after speaking to Scott Bessent, the US treasury secretary. Mr Bessent said he would announce “the toughest sanctions in history” against Tehran on Monday.
Iran did not specify which US-linked sites in the Middle East it would target, but Americans have invested in and expanded businesses substantially in the Gulf in recent years, particularly in Saudi Arabia, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates (UAE).
Iran attacked a handful of Amazon data centres in Bahrain and the UAE with drones, and threatened strikes on tech companies, shortly after the war began in February. It has otherwise avoided American targets beyond military and diplomatic facilities.
Military action against American oil companies in the Middle East would probably worry Mr Trump, who has seen his approval ratings sink amid rising petrol prices caused by the closure of the Strait of Hormuz.
The US president has repeatedly claimed that the strait would become a US territory once the war ended. On Saturday night, he posted a photo to his Truth Social account with the waterway circled, underneath the caption: “new US territory.”
![Donald Trump Truth social post of Strait of Hormuz labelled US territory](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/en-us/news/2026/08/23/TELEMMGLPICT000499261360_17874452702660_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqpSE_vT-BY72ODMakERG2yQT_CjHPKWgnv4GSTYNX8Wg.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
Iran has previously struck numerous facilities belonging to Gulf state energy companies, including the Ras Laffan LNG hub in Qatar and Aramco plants in Saudi Arabia.
Earlier on Saturday, Ebrahim Rezaei, the spokesman for Iran’s national security commission, warned Gulf states hosting American aircraft and fuel tankers that they “shouldn’t complain later” if they were targeted, including with strikes on civilian infrastructure.
Reuters also reported on Aug 5 that Abbas Araghchi, Iran’s foreign minister, had urged Gulf states to advise Mr Trump against military action and threatened retaliation on their critical energy infrastructure.
Masoud Pezeshkian, the Iranian president who has advocated making a deal to end the war, claimed on Saturday that the world had “already accepted” Tehran’s victory and that the US was “hated”.
Mr Trump has been unsuccessful in almost every move he has made to bring the war with Iran to a close.
Reluctant to resume an all-out war, and apparently lacking the resources to do so, he has turned to a campaign of economic warfare to drag the US out of the quagmire.
The decision to prolong the war by squeezing the Iranian economy will be a tough sell to Republicans and voters. Tehran has been subject to crippling economic sanctions for years and has not been brought to heel.
Combined with a wave of strikes, Tehran has refused to abandon its quest for a nuclear weapon.
Yet the US president believes that tightening those restrictions while issuing fresh curbs would “squeeze” the regime, forcing it to eventually make a deal to prevent total collapse.
summary: Iran has threatened to strike American businesses and oil interests, as well as the interests of US allies, if President Trump launches a new campaign of financial warfare and economic sanctions. Mohsen Rezai, head of Iran's national security council, warned that such a US plan would trigger an earthquake-like confrontation and stated that American economic companies around Iran would be targeted. President Trump recently announced plans for unprecedented economic warfare and isolation against Tehran to force an end to the war.
key_points: Iran threatened to strike US and Western economic companies and oil interests in response to President Trump's proposed financial warfare campaign.
Mohsen Rezai warned that US allies who join the financial campaign will also have their interests harmed and be treated as enemies.
President Trump announced plans for 'the most crushing economic operation ever' against Tehran, alongside threats of consequences for countries providing a lifeline to Iran.

Iran has previously targeted military bases, diplomatic facilities, and a handful of Amazon data centres in Bahrain and the UAE, but a direct strike on American oil companies could impact President Trump's approval ratings amid rising petrol prices.

title: Here’s why conditions on the USS Lincoln fell apart during its 270-plus days at sea
author: Bruce Golding
content:
The food shortages and other problems that sparked outrage over substandard conditions on the USS Abraham Lincoln stemmed from Iranian attacks that devastated a key Navy base on the island nation of Bahrain — leaving the ship to rely on supplies from an outpost about 2,200 miles away.
The Navy's Persian Gulf base, known as Naval Support Activity Bahrain, is the headquarters of the Fifth Fleet, which in 2004 unveiled a $25 million, state-of-the-art nerve center to support maritime military operations across the Middle East.
But the site was largely destroyed by missiles and drones that hit it February 28, the first day of President Donald Trump's war against Iran, according to The New York Times.
A short time later, the Navy began using its base on Diego Garcia — a faraway UK-administered island in the middle of the Indian Ocean, south of the Maldives — as a new logistics hub, an unidentified military official told the NYT.
The situation led to supply shortages on the Lincoln, whose crew of about 5,000 sailors and Marines has set a post-Vietnam War record of more than 270 continuous days at sea since the nuclear-powered aircraft carrier left its home port of San Diego on November 21, 2025.
![Supplies for the aircraft carrier USS Abraham Lincoln come from a Navy outpost about 2,200 miles away because Iran bombed a key base in the Persian Gulf](https://static.independent.co.uk/2026/08/20/21/14/1000w_q95.webp)
It also denied the crew the use of a nearby “liberty port” that would have provided the opportunity for shore leave.
On Thursday evening it was reported that the ship was heading back to the U.S. and was expected to arrive back in San Diego in a few weeks.
The Pentagon referred an inquiry from The Independent to U.S. Central Command, which didn't immediately respond.
A White House spokesperson re-released an earlier statement that said President Donald Trump “cares about our troops more than anyone, and he is ensuring our brave servicemembers have all the resources they need to be successful as the United States Military continues to economically strangle the Iranian regime.”
In recent weeks, relatives of some crew members went public with tales of skimpy, inedible meals, moldy showers, broken toilets and sporadic laundry service on the Lincoln.
Military mother Danielle Rappa told NBC News that her son, who's serving on the ship, “describes the overall experience as a scene out of the [Fox TV show] American Horror Story, where he feels like everybody is dead but they don't know it yet.”
One sailor went overboard August 3 wearing a life vest and was rescued after nearly an hour in the water, and others were prevented from also jumping off the ship, according to reports.
Another mother said her son had told her that there were crew members who “weren’t doing well.” She said: “One person had just given up; they weren’t reporting for duty. They were wanting to get sent home.”
She said she’d been told that conditions had improved in April after parents started complaining.
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth claimed August 13 that conditions on the Lincoln were being “completely misrepresented” in news reports, saying, “We make sure that every ship, every crew, every captain has everything we can provide them at every single moment.”
Trump also described the Lincoln's deployment as "not nearly long enough" while speaking to reporters August 14.
The president made the stunning remark a day after The Wall Street Journal reported the Navy was planning to replace the Lincoln with the USS George Washington, which the WSJ said had recently been operating in the South China Sea. On Thursday the Associated Press reported that the USS George Washington was now operating in the Middle East.
Trump’s comment also came the same day Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao in a prepared statement that the Lincoln's crew had "crushed their deployment and will return home soon as part of a planned rotation."
On August 15, Central Command — which is responsible for a region that stretches from northeast Africa into Central and South Asia — said its commander, Admiral Brad Cooper, had just completed a 10-day trip to the Middle East.
![A sailor directs a military helicopter carrying supplies to the deck of the Lincoln on August 16](https://static.independent.co.uk/2026/08/20/18/2026-08-20T144816Z_360100403_RC2PZMAB57C7_RTRMADP_3_IRAN-CRISIS-USA-CARRIER.JPG)
It included a visit to the Lincoln, where Cooper addressed the crew members and thanked them for their dedication and courage.
“The Lincoln Carrier Strike Group is a strong team of high-achieving Americans standing tall with immense, justified pride in everything they accomplished,” Cooper said in a prepared statement. “History will record this deployment as one of the most operationally intense and consequential of the modern era.”
In a social media post Thursday, Central Command, known as CENTCOM, posted a photo of sailors working on the Washington's flight deck “as the aircraft carrier transits the Arabian Sea.”
“The George Washington Carrier Strike Group is operating in Middle East during a scheduled deployment after arriving in the CENTCOM theater yesterday," the caption added.
Iran followed up its February 28 strikes against the Navy base in Bahrain with other attacks over the ensuing months, according to a late June report by the WSJ.
![The Lincoln receives fuel from the oiler USNS Henry J. Kaiser on August 17](https://static.independent.co.uk/2026/08/20/18/2026-08-19T143103Z_702194656_RC2PZMAOUIBH_RTRMADP_3_IRAN-CRISIS-USA-CARRIER.JPG)
An analysis of satellite imagery and social media video, as well as interviews with current and former service members, revealed extensive damage to the base that the Pentagon hadn't publicly acknowledged, the WSJ said.
The base's command headquarters, at least a dozen other buildings and two satellite communications terminals were all hit hard, but the military told the WSJ that no one had been killed and U.S. operations weren't significantly impacted.
Only a small staff remained on the ground after most personnel were evacuated, the WSJ said.
Iran’s attacks against the base in Bahrain and others across the region have the Pentagon considering whether to reduce America’s military presence in the Middle East after the Iran war is over, The Washington Post reported Thursday.
Shifting logistics operations away from Bahrain may have prompted Iran to fire two medium-range missiles at Diego Garcia on March 20, according to the NYT.
A Navy warship shot down one missile, and the other fell short and splashed into the Indian Ocean, the NYT said.
The U.S. looks no closer to ending the war with Iran nearly six months after Trump started it, despite repeated claims of an imminent deal. This week Trump threatened an “economic D-Day” against Tehran and any countries aiding it.
summary: Substandard conditions and food shortages on the USS Abraham Lincoln stemmed from Iranian missile and drone attacks that destroyed the Navy's key base in Bahrain on February 28. This forced the ship to rely on supplies from a faraway outpost in Diego Garcia roughly 2,200 miles away and denied the crew access to a nearby liberty port. The aircraft carrier, which surpassed 270 continuous days at sea, is now heading back to the United States and is expected to arrive in San Diego in a few weeks.
key_points: Iranian attacks on February 28 heavily damaged the Fifth Fleet's headquarters at Naval Support Activity Bahrain.
The destruction of the Bahrain base forced the Navy to shift logistics to a hub on Diego Garcia, located about 2,200 miles away.
The supply disruptions contributed to severe food shortages, moldy showers, and broken toilets for the 5,000 sailors and Marines aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln during its record-breaking deployment.
The USS Abraham Lincoln is returning to San Diego and is being replaced in the Middle East by the USS George Washington.

title: Fundraiser for repatriation of woman who died in Limerick
author: RTÉ News
content:
A fundraising campaign is under way in Limerick to help the family of 33-year-old Jady Cristine Pereira Rosa with repatriation and funeral costs.
Ms Pereira Rosa, a law graduate from Brazil, was found dead at an apartment on Lower Cecil Street on Friday morning.
Gardaí have launched a murder investigation and say they are following a line of inquiry.
It is understood that Ms Pereira Rosa was working with a cleaning company in Limerick and had many friends in the area. She has been described by those who knew her as kind and bubbly.
![Gardaí seal off the Carlton House complex on Cecil Street, Limerick](https://www.rte.ie/images/0024e055-614.jpg?ratio=1.78) 
Her body was removed from the scene to the mortuary at University Hospital Limerick, where a post-mortem examination was carried out by the State Pathologist.
Gardaí said the results of the post-mortem examination are not being released for operational reasons.
A Garda Family Liaison Officer has been assigned to support Ms Pereira Rosa's family.
Anyone with any information is asked to contact Henry Street Garda Station on 061 212400.
summary: A fundraising campaign has been launched in Limerick to cover the repatriation and funeral costs of 33-year-old Jady Cristine Pereira Rosa, who was found dead in an apartment. Gardaí have launched a murder investigation and are appealing for information from the public. A post-mortem examination has been completed, though results are being withheld for operational reasons.
key_points: A fundraiser is underway to help repatriate the body of Jady Cristine Pereira Rosa to Brazil.
The 33-year-old law graduate was found dead at an apartment on Lower Cecil Street in Limerick.
Gardaí have launched a murder investigation and appealed for witnesses to contact Henry Street Garda Station.
A post-mortem examination was carried out, but results are not being released for operational reasons.
